Introduction

The present text continues the paper “The Finitary Basis of Formal Systems and a Rigorous Construction of the Propositional Calculus with Its Models” (hereafter PC) and constructs the first-order predicate calculus (FOL) on the same finitary basis. The special metalanguage introduced in Part I of the PC paper is used unchanged: its domain of discourse is exhausted by finite words over a fixed alphabet, the basic operations and relations on them (concatenation, identity, occurrence, and word-for-word replacement), and the recursive generation of classes of words and relations between words, without appealing to infinite collections or natural numbers.

Constructing a first-order language strictly within these boundaries requires resolving two syntactic problems that did not arise in the propositional calculus.

The first problem concerns the notions of signature and arity. Unlike the propositional calculus, whose language has a single fixed vocabulary, the syntax of first-order logic is parameterized by a collection of non-logical symbols—constants, function symbols, and predicate symbols. In a set-theoretic exposition, each function and predicate symbol is assigned a natural number—its arity (number of arguments)—and the formation rules for terms and atomic formulas are written with argument lists of variable length.

Because the initial special language contains no separate class of natural numbers, function and predicate stems are generated recursively over a fixed finite alphabet in the same manner as variables, while the numerical arity function is replaced by a purely string-based construction: a string of special placeholders (slots) in parentheses, separated by commas, is adjoined to a head name. Function templates (with placeholders) are thereby formed from function stems by adjoining a string of slots, whereas function stems without attached slots simultaneously play the role of constants, realizing constants as \(0\)-ary functions; analogously, predicate templates are formed from predicate stems by adjoining a string of slots.

All function stems (constants), function templates, and predicate templates of arbitrary numbers of slots form recursively generated decidable classes of words, while a signature is specified at the metalevel as a selection from these classes possessing the antichain property: for each head name, at most one word belongs to the signature. In order to substitute arguments into a function or predicate template all at once as a list while matching the number of argument slots without counting, comma-separated term lists are generated by simultaneous recursion synchronously with strings of placeholders. A term list generated alongside the placeholder string of a given template matches it in length (is relevant to it), and forming a compound term or an atomic formula reduces to adjoining a relevant term list to the head name of the template.

The resources of the special language (a finite alphabet, operations on words, structural recursion, and structural induction) suffice in principle to construct the natural numbers themselves as a separate class of words—both in unary notation (strings of a single symbol) and in positional notation with digits and arithmetic operations (in expressive power such a metalanguage corresponds to primitive recursive arithmetic). In effect, strings of variables and strings of placeholders already constitute a unary implementation of natural numbers, and simultaneous recursion for relevant lists implements the check that their lengths coincide. Embedding a unary counter directly into positional templates avoids introducing a separate class of numeral representations and auxiliary digit arithmetic prior to constructing the syntax of the calculus, while preserving a strictly finite object alphabet; once unique readability has been proved (§ 1.2), numerical notation for arities and subscripts is introduced in § 2.1 as an abbreviation of this canon.

The second problem concerns term substitution and quantifier binding. If one uses a single stock of individual variables both at free positions in terms and under quantifiers, then word-for-word replacement from Part I of the PC paper ceases to be a sound operation on formulas: it affects bound occurrences of the variable being replaced, and variables inside the substituted term may fall within the scope of quantifiers.

To retain basic word-for-word replacement without introducing complex auxiliary predicates for admissibility of substitution and variable renaming, individual variables are partitioned already at the alphabet level into two disjoint classes—free and bound—while the propositional variables of the propositional calculus form a third class disjoint from both. Terms are built exclusively from free variables and constants, whereas bound variables are introduced solely by the quantifier attachment rule: in an already formed formula, all occurrences of a chosen free variable are replaced by a bound variable that does not yet occur in that formula. As a result, no term contains bound variables, variable capture by quantifiers upon term substitution is syntactically impossible, and the condition that a variable has no free occurrences in a formula reduces to elementary non-occurrence of one word in another. Furthermore, the independence of propositional variables from the FOL vocabulary makes it possible to obtain propositional axioms and tautologies of first-order logic by direct word-for-word substitution of FOL formulas for propositional variables in axioms and theorems of the propositional calculus.

The exposition is organized as follows. Section 1 is kept strictly finitary: in the canon of the special language, we define the classes of variables, non-logical names, positional templates, the notion of a signature as an antichain, and the classes of relevant term lists, terms, and formulas of a given signature; we establish unique readability and examine the analogy between this string-based canon and the internal representation of the Lean proof assistant kernel.

Section 2 passes to the more customary set-theoretic notation (§ 2.1), specifies the axioms, rules of inference, and derivability in the context of a finite list of hypotheses, and establishes the Renaming Lemma, the Deduction Theorem, and the basic properties of derivability. In §§ 2.4–2.5, non-finitary superstructures are built atop this finitary core of derivations—arbitrary sets of formulas, first-order theories, and countable chains of definitional extensions (the theorem on eliminability and conservativity). In Section 3, standard set theory is used to construct the semantics: structures and Tarski truth are introduced, the soundness of FOL is proved, Gödel's Completeness Theorem is stated (with its detailed proof deferred to the companion note “The Henkin Construction”), its principal corollaries (the Compactness Theorem and the Downward Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem) are derived, and two representations of the propositional calculus within first-order logic are compared—as the quantifier-free fragment of equality-free FOL and as the theory of Boolean algebras. The Conclusion traces the spiral of metatheoretic ascent from the pre-formal postulate of binarity, through the induction-free core (\(\mathsf{TC} \equiv \mathsf{Q}\)) and the finitary arithmetic stage of induction (\(\mathsf{TC} + \mathrm{Ind} \equiv \mathsf{PA} \equiv \mathsf{HF}\), with the finitary minimum \(\mathsf{PRA} \equiv_{\Pi_2} I\Sigma_1\) and \(\mathsf{EA}\)), to set-theoretic semantics (\(\mathsf{ZFC}\)).

1. Syntax of a First-Order Language

1.1. Alphabet, Variables, Templates, and Signatures

Unlike the propositional calculus, whose language has a single fixed alphabet, the syntax of first-order logic is parameterized by the choice of a signature—a collection of constants, function templates, and predicate templates. To remain within the finitary special language of Part I of the PC paper without appealing to natural numbers, the basic object alphabet is fixed once and for all: within it, all sorts of variables as well as function and predicate stems together with their positional templates are generated recursively.

A new object alphabet \(\Alf\) consisting of \(16\) symbols is fixed: \[\pp\quad \pa\quad \px\quad \pf\quad \pP\quad \pslot\quad (\quad )\quad ,\quad =\quad \neg\quad {\land}\quad {\lor}\quad {\to}\quad {\forall}\quad {\exists}\] All listed symbols are pairwise distinct and disjoint from the metasymbols of the special language. With the transition to the alphabet \(\Alf\), the notion of a word from PC changes its extension: henceforth, words everywhere mean finite strings of symbols of the alphabet \(\Alf\), and accordingly the range of the general word metavariables \(\xi, \eta, \zeta, \theta, \tau, \omega\) from § I.1 of the PC paper shifts—they now range over all words in the alphabet \(\Alf\). The basic operations and relations on words (concatenation, identity \(\equiv\), occurrence, and word-for-word replacement \(\xi[\zeta/\eta]\)) retain their definitions from § I.1 of the PC paper, but now act on words over \(\Alf\); in particular, there are no empty words.

Because the base \(7\)-symbol alphabet of the propositional calculus (with the symbol \(\pp\) for propositional variables and without the external list separator) is contained in \(\Alf\), and the formation rules for formulas and theorems in the PC paper use none of the remaining symbols of \(\Alf\), the classes of propositional variables, formulas, axioms, and theorems of PC embed unchanged into the class of words over \(\Alf\); at the same time, extending the range of the metavariables \(\xi, \eta, \zeta\) to all of \(\Alf\) allows arbitrary words of the new language to be substituted into PC formulas via the same basic replacement operation \(\xi[\zeta/\eta]\).

The comma in the alphabet \(\Alf\) serves to separate argument positions in templates and terms; moreover, by prefix-freeness of formulas (Lemma 1.7) and the editor property (§ I.1 of the PC paper), the very same comma symbol within the \(16\)-symbol alphabet \(\Alf\) (without extending it) unambiguously separates formulas in external lists of hypotheses and derivation chains (§ 2.3). Argument parentheses of metapredicates continue to be highlighted in blue (\(\mo\,\mc\)), and a compound argument of a predicate is enclosed in quotes. For compact notation of concrete words in the exposition (at the natural-language level, above the special language containing no numbers), exponential shorthand is used for consecutive repetitions of a single symbol of \(\Alf\): \(\pa^2\) for \(\pa\pa\), \(\pa^3\) for \(\pa\pa\pa\), \(\pf^2\) for \(\pf\pf\), \(\pf^3\) for \(\pf\pf\pf\), \(\pP^2\) for \(\pP\pP\), etc. (the object word itself remains the expanded string of symbols without exponents).

Equality as a logical symbol. The binary predicate symbol \(=\) does not belong to the signature: it counts among the logical symbols alongside connectives and quantifiers, is present in the language of every signature, and its axioms (reflexivity and congruence, group 3 of Definition 2.1) are logical axioms. In the semantics (Definition 3.2), the symbol \(=\) is always interpreted as the identity relation on the domain and therefore, unlike elements of the signature, is not subject to free interpretation. Unless stated otherwise, predicate calculus with equality is considered. Predicate calculus without equality is obtained by deleting the symbol \(=\) from the formula vocabulary used, the equality clause from rule F1 of Definition 1.5, and group 3 of the axioms (assuming \(\mathrm{Pred}_\Lang \neq \emptyset\), since otherwise the language contains no atomic formulas and hence no formulas at all); all results of Sections 1–3 not involving equality carry over to it unchanged.

Definition 1.1 (Classes of variables, function stems, and predicate stems). The predicates \(\PVar\mo \xi\mc\) (“propositional variable of PC”), \(\FVar\mo \xi\mc\) (“free individual variable of FOL”), \(\BVar\mo \xi\mc\) (“bound individual variable of FOL”), \(\FSym\mo \xi\mc\) (“function stem”), and \(\PSym\mo \xi\mc\) (“predicate stem”) are defined recursively:

  1. 1.

    Propositional variables (\(\PVar\)):

    1. P1.

      Basis: \(\PVar\mo \q{(\pp)}\mc\).

    2. P2.

      Rule: if \(\PVar\mo \q{(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\PVar\mo \q{(\xi\pp)}\mc\).

    3. P3.

      Closure: no other propositional variables exist.

  2. 2.

    Free individual variables (\(\FVar\)):

    1. FV1.

      Basis: \(\FVar\mo \q{(\pa)}\mc\).

    2. FV2.

      Rule: if \(\FVar\mo \q{(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\FVar\mo \q{(\xi\pa)}\mc\).

    3. FV3.

      Closure: no other free variables exist.

  3. 3.

    Bound individual variables (\(\BVar\)):

    1. BV1.

      Basis: \(\BVar\mo \q{(\px)}\mc\).

    2. BV2.

      Rule: if \(\BVar\mo \q{(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\BVar\mo \q{(\xi\px)}\mc\).

    3. BV3.

      Closure: no other bound variables exist.

  4. 4.

    Function stems (\(\FSym\)):

    1. FS1.

      Basis: \(\FSym\mo \q{(\pf)}\mc\).

    2. FS2.

      Rule: if \(\FSym\mo \q{(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\FSym\mo \q{(\xi\pf)}\mc\).

    3. FS3.

      Closure: no other function stems exist.

  5. 5.

    Predicate stems (\(\PSym\)):

    1. PS1.

      Basis: \(\PSym\mo \q{(\pP)}\mc\).

    2. PS2.

      Rule: if \(\PSym\mo \q{(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\PSym\mo \q{(\xi\pP)}\mc\).

    3. PS3.

      Closure: no other predicate stems exist.

By induction on the construction, every word of the classes \(\PVar\), \(\FVar\), \(\BVar\), \(\FSym\), and \(\PSym\) has the form \((\pp\dots\pp)\), \((\pa\dots\pa)\), \((\px\dots\px)\), \((\pf\dots\pf)\), and \((\pP\dots\pP)\), respectively, with at least one occurrence of the base symbol. Because the symbols \(\pp, \pa, \px, \pf, \pP\) are pairwise distinct, these five classes are pairwise disjoint. Moreover, the parentheses \((\) and \()\) occur in each such word only as its first and last symbol, so no word of any of the five classes \(\PVar\), \(\FVar\), \(\BVar\), \(\FSym\), \(\PSym\) is a proper subword of another word of any of these classes; thus word-for-word replacement \(\xi[\zeta/\eta]\) of any such word acts cleanly without affecting the others. Words of the class \(\FSym\) serve simultaneously as head names of function templates and as constants (realizing constants as \(0\)-ary functions), whereas words of the class \(\PSym\) are used only as head names of predicate templates.

Once these classes are defined, restricted metavariables are assigned to them:

  • to the class \(\PVar\)—the lowercase Latin letters \(p, q, r\) (as in the PC paper);

  • to the class \(\FVar\)—the lowercase Latin letters from the beginning of the alphabet \(a, b, c, d\);

  • to the class \(\BVar\)—the lowercase Latin letters from the end of the alphabet \(x, y, z, u, v, w\);

  • to the class \(\FSym\)—the uppercase Latin letters \(C, D\).

Next, using the classes \(\FSym\) and \(\PSym\), the classes of function and predicate templates are defined within the special language.

Definition 1.2 (Function and predicate templates). The classes \(\FTpl\) (“function template”) and \(\PTpl\) (“predicate template”) are defined recursively:

  1. 1.

    Function templates (\(\FTpl\)):

    1. FT1.

      Basis: \(\FTpl\mo \q{C(\pslot)}\mc\).

    2. FT2.

      Rule: if \(\FTpl\mo \q{C(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\FTpl\mo \q{C(\xi,\pslot)}\mc\).

    3. FT3.

      Closure: no other function templates exist.

  2. 2.

    Predicate templates (\(\PTpl\)):

    1. PT1.

      Basis: if \(\PSym\mo \eta\mc\), then \(\PTpl\mo \q{\eta(\pslot)}\mc\).

    2. PT2.

      Rule: if \(\PSym\mo \eta\mc\) and \(\PTpl\mo \q{\eta(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\PTpl\mo \q{\eta(\xi,\pslot)}\mc\).

    3. PT3.

      Closure: no other predicate templates exist.

By induction on the construction, the class of function templates \(\FTpl\) consists of words of the form \((\pf\dots\pf)(\pslot,\dots,\pslot)\) (one or more placeholders \(\pslot\) separated by commas inside the second pair of parentheses), e.g., \((\pf)(\pslot)\), \((\pf)(\pslot,\pslot)\), \((\pf^2)(\pslot,\pslot,\pslot)\), and the class of predicate templates \(\PTpl\) consists of words of the form \((\pP\dots\pP)(\pslot,\dots,\pslot)\), e.g., \((\pP)(\pslot)\), \((\pP^2)(\pslot,\pslot)\).

To the newly defined classes \(\FTpl\) and \(\PTpl\) are assigned the corresponding restricted metavariables:

  • to the class \(\FTpl\)—the uppercase Latin letters \(F, G, H\) (so each denotes a function template of the form \(C\xi\) already together with its parenthesized string of placeholders);

  • to the class \(\PTpl\)—the uppercase Latin letters \(P, Q\) (denoting a predicate template of the form \(\eta\xi\) already together with its parenthesized string of placeholders).

The classes \(\FTpl\) and \(\PTpl\) are decidable: to test whether a word belongs to \(\FTpl\) (or \(\PTpl\)), it suffices to split off the initial word of \(\FSym\) (respectively \(\PSym\)), which is uniquely determined by its first pair of symbols and the position of the first closing parenthesis, and verify that the remaining part is a string of alternating symbols \(\pslot\) and commas inside a pair of parentheses \((\) and \()\).

Every word of the classes \(\FSym\), \(\FTpl\), and \(\PTpl\) begins with a unique word of \(\FSym\) or \(\PSym\)—its head name: for both a function stem (constant) \(C\) and a function template \(C\xi\), the head name is the function stem \(C\) (built from \(\pf\)), whereas for a predicate template \(\eta\xi\), the head name is the predicate stem \(\eta\) (built from \(\pP\)). A function stem \(C\) without attached placeholders acts as a \(0\)-ary function template (a constant).

Definition 1.3 (Signature). A signature \(\Lang\) is a subclass (selection) of words from the classes \(\FSym\), \(\FTpl\), and \(\PTpl\) possessing the antichain property: no two distinct words of the signature \(\Lang\) share a common head name (thus, for each function stem \(C\), the signature \(\Lang\) contains either the stem \(C\) itself as a constant or at most one function template of the form \(C\xi\), and for each predicate stem \(\eta\), at most one predicate template of the form \(\eta\xi\)). Membership of a word \(\eta\) in the signature \(\Lang\) is denoted by the predicate \(\Lang\mo \eta\mc\).

The choice of signature is made at the metalevel and requires introducing neither a new syntactic separator nor a special class of signatures: in particular, an empty signature (the pure language of equality), a finite selection of words, and (in Section 3, where finitary restrictions are lifted) an infinite antichain of words from \(\FSym\), \(\FTpl\), and \(\PTpl\) are all permitted. For a finite (or decidable) selection \(\Lang\), testing the predicate \(\Lang\mo \eta\mc\) terminates in finitely many steps, which ensures the decidability of the language in Sections 1–2. The antichain property guarantees that for any head name \(C\) (or predicate stem \(\eta\)) occurring in the signature \(\Lang\), there is exactly one word in \(\Lang\) with that head name: for example, a single signature cannot simultaneously contain the constant \(C\) and the function template \(C(\pslot)\), two function templates \(C(\pslot)\) and \(C(\pslot,\pslot)\), or predicate templates \(\eta(\pslot)\) and \(\eta(\pslot,\pslot)\). The layout of the basic syntactic classes in the alphabet \(\Alf\) and of the signature antichain \(\Lang\) is shown in Fig. 1.

1.2. Terms, Relevant Lists, and Formulas of a Signature

Henceforth, let a signature \(\Lang\) (in the sense of Definition 1.3) be fixed. Words of the language of this signature fall into two primary syntactic classes: terms, denoting objects of the domain, and formulas, expressing assertions about those objects. To substitute arguments into function and predicate templates all at once as a list and match its length to the string of placeholders without using numbers, term lists are generated by simultaneous recursion with placeholder strings.

Definition 1.4 (Terms and relevant term lists). The predicate \(\Term\mo \xi\mc\) (“the word \(\xi\) is a term of signature \(\Lang\)”) and the relation \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \xi\mc\) (“the term list \(\tau\) is relevant to the placeholder string \(\xi\)”) are defined by simultaneous recursion:

  1. Tm1.

    Basis of terms: \(\Term\mo a\mc\); if \(\Lang\mo C\mc\), then \(\Term\mo C\mc\).

  2. Tm2.

    Single-element term list: if \(\Term\mo \eta\mc\), then \(\Rel\mo \q{(\eta)} \,;\, \q{(\pslot)}\mc\).

  3. Tm3.

    Appending a term to a list: if \(\Term\mo \eta\mc\) and \(\Rel\mo \q{(\tau)} \,;\, \q{(\xi)}\mc\), then \(\Rel\mo \q{(\eta,\tau)} \,;\, \q{(\pslot,\xi)}\mc\).

  4. Tm4.

    Applying a function template: if \(\Lang\mo \q{C\xi}\mc\) and \(\Rel\mo \tau \,;\, \xi\mc\), then \(\Term\mo \q{C\tau}\mc\).

  5. Tm5.

    Closure: no other terms and no other pairs in the relation \(\Rel\) exist.

The restricted metavariables \(T, R\) are assigned to the class \(\Term\).

By induction on the construction (rules Tm1–Tm4), the general form of words in the class \(\Term\) is established: every term of signature \(\Lang\) is either a free variable of the form \((\pa\dots\pa)\), or a constant of the form \((\pf\dots\pf)\) from \(\Lang\), or a compound term of the form \((\pf\dots\pf)(T_1,\dots,T_n)\), where the template \((\pf\dots\pf)(\pslot,\dots,\pslot)\) with the same number of placeholders belongs to \(\Lang\) and each argument \(T_1, \dots, T_n\) is itself a term of one of these three kinds; no other terms exist. An example of a parse tree of a term is shown in Fig. 2.

Definition 1.5 (Formulas of the language of signature \(\Lang\)). The predicate \(\Form\mo \xi\mc\) (“the word \(\xi\) is a formula of signature \(\Lang\)”) is defined recursively:

  1. F1.

    Atomic formulas: \(\Form\mo \q{(T = R)}\mc\); if \(\PSym\mo \eta\mc\), \(\Lang\mo \q{\eta\xi}\mc\), and \(\Rel\mo \tau \,;\, \xi\mc\), then \(\Form\mo \q{\eta\tau}\mc\).

  2. F2.

    Negation: if \(\Form\mo \xi\mc\), then \(\Form\mo \q{\neg\xi}\mc\).

  3. F3.

    Binary connectives: if \(\Form\mo \xi\mc\) and \(\Form\mo \eta\mc\), then \[\Form\mo \q{(\xi\land\eta)}\mc,\qquad \Form\mo \q{(\xi\lor\eta)}\mc,\qquad \Form\mo \q{(\xi\to\eta)}\mc.\]

  4. F4.

    Quantifiers: if \(\Form\mo \xi\mc\) and the variable \(x\) does not occur in the word \(\xi\), then \[\Form\mo \q{\forall x\,\xi[x/a]}\mc,\qquad \Form\mo \q{\exists x\,\xi[x/a]}\mc.\]

  5. F5.

    Closure: no other formulas exist.

The restricted metavariables \(\varphi, \psi, \chi\) are assigned to the class \(\Form\) (whereas calligraphic \(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}\) continue to refer to formulas of PC). The class of all formulas \(\Form\) for a fixed signature \(\Lang\) is called the language of signature \(\Lang\) and is denoted by \(\mathcal{L}_\Lang\). A diagram showing the inclusion and separation of the syntactic classes of signature \(\Lang\) (in the notation of Section 2) is given later in § 2.2 in Fig. 4. An example of a parse tree of a formula is shown in Fig. 3.

Henceforth, the metasigns \(\circ, \bullet\) denote an arbitrary binary connective among \(\land, \lor, \to\), and the metasign \(\mathsf{Q}\) denotes a quantifier among \(\forall, \exists\).

To prove unique readability of terms and formulas, auxiliary classes of words are introduced that admit arbitrary individual variables in argument positions, and disjointness of classes together with prefix-freeness are established.

Definition 1.6 (Quasiterms and quasiformulas). The classes of quasiterms \(\Term^*\) and quasiformulas \(\Form^*\) and the relation \(\Rel^*\) for lists of quasiterms are defined by the same rules Tm1–Tm5 and F1–F5 of Definitions 1.4 and 1.5 with two relaxations: in Tm1, arbitrary individual variables of \(\FVar\) and \(\BVar\) are permitted, and in F4, for any \(x \in \BVar\) and \(\psi \in \Form^*\), one sets \(\Form^*\mo \q{\forall x\,\psi}\mc\) and \(\Form^*\mo \q{\exists x\,\psi}\mc\).

By induction on the construction, the classes \(\Term^*\) and \(\Form^*\) are closed under word-for-word replacement \(\xi[u/a]\) of any free variable \(a \in \FVar\) by an arbitrary variable \(u \in \FVar \cup \BVar\) (such a replacement does not affect quantifier prefixes \(\mathsf{Q}x\), where \(x \in \BVar\)). In particular, for \(\psi \in \Form^*\) and \(x \in \BVar\), one has \(\psi[x/a] \in \Form^*\), whence \(\Term \subseteq \Term^*\) and \(\Form \subseteq \Form^*\).

Lemma 1.7 (Separation of classes and initial subwords).

  1. (a)

    The classes \(\Term\) and \(\Form\) are disjoint.

  2. (b)

    No word of the class \(\Term\) or \(\Form\) is a proper initial subword of another word of the classes \(\Term\) and \(\Form\).

Proof.

Because \(\Term \subseteq \Term^*\) and \(\Form \subseteq \Form^*\), it suffices to prove both statements for \(\Term^*\) and \(\Form^*\).

(a) Every word of the classes \(\FVar\), \(\BVar\), \(\FSym\), and \(\PSym\) begins with the parenthesis \((\) followed by \(\pa\), \(\px\), \(\pf\), or \(\pP\), respectively. Therefore every quasiterm of \(\Term^*\) begins with \((\) whose second symbol is \(\pa\), \(\px\), or \(\pf\). Every quasiformula of \(\Form^*\), on the other hand, begins either with one of the symbols \(\neg, \forall, \exists\), or with \((\) whose second symbol is \(\pP\) (for predicate formulas) or the initial symbol of a quasiterm or quasiformula (for \((T = R)\) and \((\varphi \circ \psi)\)), i.e., again one of \((, \neg, \forall, \exists\). Since the first two symbols of a quasiterm and a quasiformula never coincide, the classes \(\Term^*\) and \(\Form^*\) are disjoint.

(b) By simultaneous structural induction on the construction of words in \(\Term^*\), \(\Rel^*\), and \(\Form^*\), we show that no word \(\xi\) of \(\Term^*\) or \(\Form^*\) is a proper initial subword of another word \(\eta\) of \(\Term^*\) or \(\Form^*\), and that for a fixed placeholder string \(\zeta\), no list \(\tau\) with \(\Rel^*\mo \tau ; \zeta\mc\) is a proper initial subword of another list \(\theta\) with \(\Rel^*\mo \theta ; \zeta\mc\). If one of two words is a proper initial subword of the other, their first two symbols coincide; moreover, all formation rules reduce to three structural mechanisms that preserve prefix-freeness by the properties of words from § I.1 of the PC paper:

  1. 1.

    Parenthesized basic atoms (\(\FVar\), \(\BVar\), \(\FSym\), \(\PSym\)): the closing parenthesis \()\) occurs in each word of these classes only as its last symbol, so none of them can be a proper initial subword of another; in particular, this handles the basis Tm1 for variables.

  2. 2.

    Prefix composition (\(\neg\varphi\), \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\varphi\), as well as \(C\) in Tm1, \(C\tau\) in Tm4, and \(\eta\tau\) in F1): if the left parts of two words belong to an already prefix-free class, then by prefix-freeness (and left-cancellation of word concatenation) those left parts coincide and cancel, transferring the comparison to the right parts. Specifically:

    • in negations \(\neg\varphi\), \(\neg\psi\) (F2), \(\neg\) cancels, and in quantified words \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\varphi\), \(\mathsf{Q}y\,\psi\) (F4), after canceling \(\mathsf{Q}\), prefix-freeness of \(\BVar\) forces \(x \equiv y\), which cancels and reduces the task to the induction hypothesis for \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\);

    • in words beginning with \((\pf\) (Tm1, Tm4) or \((\pP\) (F1), prefix-freeness of \(\FSym\) and \(\PSym\) forces the head names to coincide, and by the antichain property of the signature \(\Lang\) (Definition 1.3), the shared head name occurs in \(\Lang\) within a unique word—either the constant \(C\) (in which case both words equal \(C\)) or a unique template with placeholder string \(\zeta\), in which case canceling the head name reduces the task to the lists \(\tau, \theta\) with the common placeholder string \(\zeta\).

  3. 3.

    Parenthesizing with a separator (lists \(\q{(T)}\) and \(\q{(T,\tau)}\) in Tm2–Tm3, equalities \((T = R)\) in F1, and binary quasiformulas \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) in F3): after canceling the outer opening parenthesis \((\), the first components are initial subwords of the same word and coincide by the induction hypothesis (and by part (a), a quasiterm \(T\) from \((T = R)\) cannot coincide with a quasiformula \(\varphi\) from \((\varphi \circ \psi)\), so both compared words are of the same kind). After canceling the first component, in a single-element list \(\q{(T)}\) only the closing parenthesis \()\) remains, precluding proper extension; in equalities and binary quasiformulas, the separators (\(=\) or connective \(\circ\)) coincide and cancel, after which the induction hypothesis forces the second components and the final parenthesis \()\) to coincide; finally, in compound lists \(\q{(T,\tau)}\) and \(\q{(R,\theta)}\) (Tm3), after canceling the first component and the comma, adjoining \((\) on the left returns the comparison to the lists \(\q{(\tau)}\) and \(\q{(\theta)}\) for a shorter placeholder string, completing the induction. ∎

Proposition 1.8 (Unique readability of terms, lists, and formulas).

  1. (a)

    Every term \(T\) has exactly one of the following forms: a free variable \(a\); a constant \(C\) of signature \(\Lang\); a word \(C\tau\) for a unique function template \(F \equiv C\zeta\) of signature \(\Lang\) and a unique term list \(\tau\) satisfying \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \zeta\mc\). Moreover, for any list \(\tau\) satisfying \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \zeta\mc\), the terms occurring in it are uniquely recovered: if \(\zeta \equiv \q{(\pslot)}\), then \(\tau \equiv \q{(T)}\) for a unique term \(T\); if \(\zeta \equiv \q{(\pslot,\omega)}\), then \(\tau \equiv \q{(R,\theta)}\) for uniquely determined term \(R\) and list \(\q{(\theta)}\) with \(\Rel\mo \q{(\theta)} ; \q{(\omega)}\mc\).

  2. (b)

    Every formula has exactly one of the following forms: \(\eta\tau\) (\(\Lang\mo P\mc\), \(P \equiv \eta\zeta\), \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \zeta\mc\)); \((T = R)\); \(\neg\varphi\); \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) (\(\circ\) is one of \(\land, \lor, \to\)); \(\forall x\,\chi\); \(\exists x\,\chi\). Moreover, all constituents (predicate template \(P\), relevant list \(\tau\), terms \(T, R\), connective \(\circ\), subformulas \(\varphi, \psi\), bound variable \(x\), and quantifier body \(\chi\)) are uniquely determined. In the quantified case, \(\chi \equiv \varphi[x/a]\) for some formula \(\varphi \in \Form\) and free variable \(a \in \FVar\) (and for any free variable \(b\) not occurring in \(\chi\), one has \(\chi[b/x] \equiv \varphi[b/a]\) and \(\chi \equiv (\chi[b/x])[x/b]\)).

Proof.

For terms, a free variable begins with \((\pa\), whereas a constant and a function term begin with \((\pf\). In a word \(C\tau\), the closing parenthesis of the head name \(C\) is immediately followed by the opening parenthesis \((\) of the list \(\tau\), whereas in a constant \(C\) (\(\Lang\mo C\mc\)) the word ends at that closing parenthesis (in agreement with the antichain property of \(\Lang\), which uniquely determines a word of \(\Lang\) from its head name). If \(\q{(T,\tau)} \equiv \q{(R,\theta)}\) with \(\Rel\mo \q{(T,\tau)} ; \q{(\pslot,\zeta)}\mc\) and \(\Rel\mo \q{(R,\theta)} ; \q{(\pslot,\zeta)}\mc\), then after canceling the initial parenthesis \((\), the identity \(T \equiv R\) follows from Lemma 1.7 (b), after which canceling \(T\) and the comma gives \(\tau \equiv \theta\), and hence \(\q{(\tau)} \equiv \q{(\theta)}\). For formulas, the initial symbol pairs \((\pP\) (for \(\eta\tau\)), \(((\), \((\neg\), \((\forall\), \((\exists\) and the initial symbols \(\neg, \forall, \exists\) immediately separate all cases except \((T = R)\) and \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) (in both of these cases the second symbol may be \((\); they cannot coincide, since after canceling the outer parenthesis, \((T = R)\) begins with the term \(T\) whereas \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) begins with the formula \(\varphi\), which is impossible by Lemma 1.7). Uniqueness of the constituents in each case follows from Lemma 1.7 (b) (for \(\forall x\,\chi\) and \(\exists x\,\chi\), in the classes \(\Term^*\) and \(\Form^*\)). In the quantified case, by Definition 1.5 (F4) we have \(\chi \equiv \varphi[x/a]\), where \(x\) does not occur in the formula \(\varphi\); for any free variable \(b\) not occurring in \(\chi\), every occurrence of \(x\) in \(\chi\) arose from an occurrence of \(a\) in \(\varphi\), so \(\chi[b/x] \equiv \varphi[b/a]\) and \((\chi[b/x])[x/b] \equiv \chi\).∎

Lemma 1.9 (Closure of terms and formulas under substitution). For any terms \(R, T \in \Term\), formula \(\varphi \in \Form\), and free variable \(a \in \FVar\), one has \(\Term\mo \q{R[T/a]}\mc\) and \(\Form\mo \q{\varphi[T/a]}\mc\), and the word \(\varphi[T/a]\) contains the same number of occurrences of connectives and quantifiers (\(\neg, \land, \lor, \to, \forall, \exists\)) as \(\varphi\).

Proof.

Note first that no term in \(\Term\) contains the connective or quantifier symbols \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to, \forall, \exists\), and words of the classes \(\FVar\), \(\BVar\), \(\FSym\), \(\PSym\) are not proper subwords of one another, so word-for-word replacements of variables do not affect other symbol classes and create no spurious occurrences.

Closure of \(\Term\) under substitution \([T/a]\) (together with closure of \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \xi\mc\) under componentwise replacement \(\tau[T/a]\)) is proved by simultaneous structural induction on rules Tm1–Tm4: if \(R \equiv a\), then \(R[T/a] \equiv T \in \Term\); if \(R \not\equiv a\) and \(R\) belongs to the basis Tm1, then \(R[T/a] \equiv R \in \Term\); rules Tm2–Tm4 carry over by the induction hypothesis, since \(a\) occurs neither in \(\pslot\) nor in head names from \(\FSym\).

Closure of \(\Form\) and preservation of the number of connectives and quantifiers are proved by induction on the number \(k\) of occurrences of the symbols \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to, \forall, \exists\) in the formula \(\varphi\) (simultaneously for all \(a \in \FVar\) and \(T \in \Term\)):

  • \(k = 0\) (F1): \(\varphi\) has the form \((R_1 = R_2)\) or \(\eta\tau\) (\(\eta \in \PSym\)); by what has already been proved for \(\Term\) and \(\Rel\), the word \(\varphi[T/a]\) belongs to \(\Form\) and contains no connectives or quantifiers.

  • Step F2 (\(\varphi \equiv \neg\psi\)) and F3 (\(\varphi \equiv (\psi_1 \circ \psi_2)\)): the induction hypothesis for \(\psi\), \(\psi_1\), \(\psi_2\) yields \(\psi[T/a], \psi_1[T/a], \psi_2[T/a] \in \Form\) with the same number of connectives and quantifiers.

  • Step F4 (\(\varphi \equiv \mathsf{Q}y\,\psi[y/b]\), where \(\psi \in \Form\) contains \(k - 1\) occurrences of connectives and quantifiers and \(y \in \BVar\) does not occur in \(\psi\)): if \(b \equiv a\), then \(a\) does not occur in \(\psi[y/a]\), so \(\varphi[T/a] \equiv \varphi \in \Form\). Suppose \(b \not\equiv a\).

    • If \(b\) does not occur in \(T\), then since \(y \in \BVar\) also does not occur in \(T\), the word-for-word replacements \([T/a]\) and \([y/b]\) commute on \(\psi\): \((\psi[y/b])[T/a] \equiv (\psi[T/a])[y/b]\). By the induction hypothesis, \(\psi[T/a] \in \Form\) has \(k - 1\) connectives and quantifiers, and \(y\) does not occur in \(\psi[T/a]\). By rule F4, \(\varphi[T/a] \equiv \mathsf{Q}y\,(\psi[T/a])[y/b] \in \Form\) (with \(k\) connectives and quantifiers).

    • If \(b\) occurs in \(T\), choose a free variable \(c \in \FVar\) that occurs neither in \(\psi\) nor in \(T\) and is distinct from \(a\) and \(b\). By the induction hypothesis (at \(k - 1\)) for the substitution \([c/b]\), we have \(\psi' \equiv \psi[c/b] \in \Form\) with \(k - 1\) connectives and quantifiers, \(y\) does not occur in \(\psi'\), and \(\psi[y/b] \equiv (\psi[c/b])[y/c] \equiv \psi'[y/c]\). Because \(c\) does not occur in \(T\) and \(c \not\equiv a\), the previous case applies to \(\psi'[y/c]\): \((\psi'[y/c])[T/a] \equiv (\psi'[T/a])[y/c]\) and \(\varphi[T/a] \equiv \mathsf{Q}y\,(\psi'[T/a])[y/c] \in \Form\). ∎

Unique readability and Lemma 1.9 guarantee the decidability of the classes \(\PVar\), \(\FVar\), \(\BVar\), \(\FSym\), \(\PSym\), \(\FTpl\), \(\PTpl\), and—when \(\Lang\) is a decidable selection—also the decidability of \(\Term\), \(\Rel\), and \(\Form\), as well as the well-definedness of definitions of functions and predicates by structural recursion. In particular, for a quantified formula \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi\), passing to the quantifier body can be done by replacing \(x\) with an arbitrary free variable \(b\) not occurring in \(\chi\), obtaining by Proposition 1.8 (b) and Lemma 1.9 a formula \(\chi[b/x] \in \Form\) of strictly smaller complexity (with one fewer connective or quantifier).

Remark 1.10 (Bottom-up reduction and generation via word-for-word replacements). Prefix-freeness and unique readability admit a transparent algorithmic interpretation via the basic operation of word-for-word replacement \(\xi[\zeta/\eta]\) from § I.1 of the PC paper, if one chooses the basic variable \((\pa)\) as the reference term and the propositional variable \((\pp)\) as the reference atom for formulas. By successive bottom-up replacements along the construction tree, every individual variable and every constant \(C\) of signature \(\Lang\) (\(\Lang\mo C\mc\)) is replaced by \((\pa)\); elementary function calls of the form \(C((\pa),\dots,(\pa))\) (for templates in \(\Lang\)) then collapse back to \((\pa)\); elementary atomic formulas \(\zeta((\pa),\dots,(\pa))\) and \(((\pa) = (\pa))\) are replaced by \((\pp)\); and finally the constructs \(\neg(\pp)\), \(\mathsf{Q}(\pa)\,(\pp)\), and \(((\pp) \circ (\pp))\) are successively reduced to \((\pp)\). Consequently, every quasiterm reduces to \((\pa)\) and every quasiformula reduces to \((\pp)\). The antichain property of \(\Lang\) and the closure of parenthesized constructs from the proof of Lemma 1.7 ensure that elementary subwords subject to reduction cannot overlap across the boundary between a quasiterm or quasiformula \(\xi\) and a non-empty word \(\omega\) adjoined on the right: after reducing the initial subword \(\xi\) to \((\pa)\) or \((\pp)\), the word \(\xi\omega\) leaves a word of the form \((\pa)\theta\) or \((\pp)\theta\), to which no rule of reduction to a single reference symbol \((\pa)\) or \((\pp)\) can apply, since compound constructs always begin with one of \((, \neg, \forall, \exists\) or with a head name from \(\FSym\) or \(\PSym\).

Dually, word-for-word replacement \(\xi[T/a]\) makes it possible to generate the exact same classes \(\Term\) and \(\Form\) without the placeholder symbol \(\pslot\) in the alphabet and without the auxiliary relation \(\Rel\): it suffices in the templates \(\FTpl\) and \(\PTpl\) to write, instead of the placeholder string \((\pslot,\dots,\pslot)\), the canonical list of pairwise distinct free variables \(((\pa)), ((\pa),(\pa^2)), ((\pa),(\pa^2),(\pa^3)), \dots\) (generated recursively by adjoining the next variable \((\eta\pa)\) after the last variable \((\eta)\)), include the templates belonging to \(\Lang\) directly in the basis of terms and atomic formulas, and generate compound terms and predicate atomic formulas from them by the single-variable substitution rule \(\xi \mapsto \xi[T/a]\) (under sequential substitution of multiple arguments, name collisions are avoided via fresh intermediate variables just as in § II.2 of the PC paper). In that representation, however, one and the same term or atom receives infinitely many distinct construction trees, whereas the construction with nameless placeholders \(\pslot\) and lists \(\Rel\) assembles each compound expression from its immediate subwords in a single step and thereby immediately identifies the construction tree with the parse tree.

1.3. Translating the Formal Canon into the Internal Representation of the Lean Proof Assistant

The mechanisms that emerged in the rigorous construction of FOL syntax over a finite alphabet—the separation of free and bound variables, the prohibition of bound variables occurring free in terms, and the control of arity and unique declaration of signature names—have a close analogue in the internal architecture of modern interactive theorem provers (proof assistants), in particular in the kernel of Lean (Lean 4). However, Lean's kernel is typed, and the separation into bvar and fvar (the locally nameless representation) is a device of internal expression representation rather than a partition of the source text alphabet.

The key difference lies in the boundary between linear text and syntactic trees. In the present exposition, the formal system is built directly from flat strings in the alphabet \(\Alf\), so all issues of separators, parentheses, and unique readability (Lemma 1.7 and Proposition 1.8) are resolved within the syntactic foundation itself. In Lean, parsing a text file with parentheses and commas is relegated to an external parser and elaborator, whereas the trusted logical kernel operates directly on already parsed trees—values of the inductive expression type Expr. Within this representation, the canon of Section 1 translates into Lean kernel constructs as follows.

1. Separation of \(\FVar\) and \(\BVar\): locally nameless representation. In Lean's kernel type Expr, variables are likewise separated into two disjoint constructors (the so-called locally nameless representation):

  • free variables \(\FVar\) correspond to the constructor Expr.fvar, storing a unique free-variable identifier; only such variables appear in open terms and contexts of hypotheses;

  • bound variables \(\BVar\) correspond to the constructor Expr.bvar carrying a de Bruijn index \(k\), indicating the number of enclosing quantifiers (counted upward in the tree from the given occurrence; e.g., \(\texttt{bvar}~0\) refers to the nearest binding quantifier).

In a well-formed Lean expression, just as in formulas of the class \(\Form\) of Definition 1.5, no unbound occurrences of bvar exist. Rule F4 of quantifier attachment \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) corresponds in Lean's kernel to the built-in operation abstract: it replaces all occurrences of a given free variable fvar in the tree \(\varphi\) by the corresponding de Bruijn index bvar, and wraps the result in the quantifier constructor Expr.forallE (for the existential quantifier \(\exists x\,\varphi[x/a]\), the same abstract operation is used together with the \(\lambda\)-abstraction constructor Expr.lam and the predicate Exists). The converse passage—substituting a term \(T\) when instantiating a quantifier—corresponds to the operation instantiate, which replaces bvar \(0\) by the tree of the term \(T\). Because no bvar-closed tree of a term \(T\) contains unbound bvars, variable capture by quantifiers during substitution is syntactically impossible, and de Bruijn indices eliminate the need to choose names for bound variables.

2. Templates, relevant lists, and the antichain property: currying and the environment. In place of positional templates from \(\FTpl \cup \PTpl\) and the simultaneous recursion \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \xi\mc\), Lean's kernel uses currying and a typed declaration table—the Environment:

  • the domain of discourse is fixed as a type \(U\) (of type Type), and elements of the signature are declared as constants in the Environment (expressions Expr.const); the antichain property of Definition 1.3 corresponds to name uniqueness in the environment: each head name may be declared in Environment only once with a single type;

  • templates of arbitrary length are replaced by iterated function types (built with the same constructor Expr.forallE without dependency): a constant \(C \in \FSym\) (as a \(0\)-ary function) corresponds to type \(U\), a function template \(F \in \FTpl\) of the form \(C\xi\) with \(n\) placeholders corresponds to type \(U \to \dots \to U\) (\(n\) arrows), and a predicate template \(P \in \PTpl\) of the form \(\eta\xi\) with \(n\) placeholders corresponds to type \(U \to \dots \to U \to \texttt{Prop}\);

  • relevant term lists \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \xi\mc\) and their attachment to a head name (\(C\tau\) for \(F \equiv C\xi\)) are replaced by nested binary function application Expr.app: the expression \(C(T_1, \dots, T_n)\) is represented in memory by the tree \[\texttt{app}\bigl(\dots\,\texttt{app}(\texttt{app}(C,\, T_1),\, T_2)\dots,\, T_n\bigr),\] and consistency of the number of arguments with the string of placeholders (the condition \(\Rel\mo \tau ; \xi\mc\)) is checked by the kernel's type system via the number of arrows in the declared type of the constant.

The table below compares the key constructs of the string canon of Section 1 with their analogues in the Lean 4 kernel.

String canon (Section 1)Lean 4 kernel (Expr, Environment)
Word in the \(16\)-symbol alphabet \(\Alf\); Lemma 1.7 and Proposition 1.8Value of tree type Expr (text parsing is delegated to an external parser)
Free variable \(a \in \FVar\)Constructor Expr.fvar
Bound variable \(x \in \BVar\)Constructor Expr.bvar (de Bruijn index)
Quantifier attachment \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) (F4)Operation abstract and constructor Expr.forallE
Quantifier instantiation \((\chi[b/x])[T/b]\) (\(b \notin \chi\), Prop. 1.8 (b))Operation instantiate
Signature \(\Lang\) as an antichain in \(\FSym \cup \FTpl \cup \PTpl\)Uniquely declared constants Expr.const in Environment
Number of slots \(\pslot\) in string \(\xi\) of template \(F \equiv C\xi\) / \(P \equiv \eta\xi\)Number of arrows in type \(U \to \dots \to U\) or \(U \to \dots \to \texttt{Prop}\)
Applying template \(F \equiv C\xi\) to relevant list \(\tau\) (term \(C\tau\))Chain of binary nodes Expr.app with type checking
Equality \((T = R)\), connectives \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to\)Applications of built-in constants Eq, Not, And, Or and constructor Expr.forallE

2. The Predicate Calculus

2.1. First-Order Language

In the preceding section, following the finitary canon established in the description of the language of PC, it was shown how the language of first-order predicate calculus is specified over a finite alphabet using the small arsenal of special-language tools defined in Part I of the PC paper. For a clearer overview of the whole picture, a more customary and compact description of the language of FOL is given below, employing set-theoretic notation and freer notational conventions.

Thus, the logical apparatus of FOL is taken to include the standard logical connectives \(\neg,\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\) (where \(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\) abbreviates \((\varphi \to \psi) \land (\psi \to \varphi)\)), the quantifier symbols \(\forall,\exists\), and the equality symbol \(=\). As in § 1.2, an arbitrary quantifier (\(\forall\) or \(\exists\)) is denoted by the metasign \(\mathsf{Q}\) (to distinguish it from the predicate letter \(Q\)). It is also assumed that \(p,q,r\) range over propositional variables of PC, and \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\dots\) range over formulas of PC.

Further, the letters \(a,b,c,\dots\) from the beginning of the Latin alphabet are retained for arbitrary free individual variables (\(\FVar\)), and the letters \(x,y,z\) and nearby letters from the end of the Latin alphabet are retained for arbitrary bound individual variables (\(\BVar\)). Let \(\mathrm{Const}_\Lang\) be the set of constant symbols, \(\mathrm{Func}_\Lang\) the set of function symbols, and \(\mathrm{Pred}_\Lang\) the set of predicate symbols. Their union \(\Sigma=\mathrm{Const}_\Lang\cup\mathrm{Func}_\Lang\cup\mathrm{Pred}_\Lang\) constitutes the signature of the language under consideration. Contentually, these three sets are specified as selections from the classes \(\FSym\), \(\FTpl\), and \(\PTpl\), so \(\Sigma\) is at most countable (since \(\FSym\), \(\FTpl\), \(\PTpl\) consist of words over the finite alphabet \(\Alf\)). Disjointness of the three sets \(\mathrm{Const}_\Lang, \mathrm{Func}_\Lang, \mathrm{Pred}_\Lang\) holds automatically; the substantive requirement of Definition 1.3 is the antichain condition (“one head name—one arity”): a signature \(\Lang\) cannot simultaneously contain a constant and a function template, or two templates of different arities, with the same head name.

As before, the metavariables \(C,D\) are assigned to constant symbols, \(F,G,H\) to function symbols, \(P,Q\) to predicate symbols, \(T,R\) to terms, and \(\varphi,\chi,\psi,\alpha,\beta\) to formulas, with \(\alpha,\beta\) used primarily for non-logical axioms (thus lowercase Latin letters always denote variables of one sort or another, uppercase Latin letters denote non-logical symbols and terms, and the listed Greek letters—disjoint from the six general word metavariables \(\xi,\eta,\zeta,\theta,\tau,\omega\) of § 1.1—denote formulas). Moreover, various accents and numerical subscripts may be attached to any letter symbols to ensure an adequate supply (\(a_1,b'',C_1,\hat D_0,F_0,G'_4,P_1,Q_8,T_1,R'\), etc.).

Function and predicate symbols have a definite arity (\(n \ge 1\), or \(n = 0\) for constants), which in the canon of Section 1 is specified by a string of placeholders or a list of distinct free variables in parentheses immediately following the symbol: \(F(a), G(a,b), P(a,b,c)\), etc. Accordingly, the exposition employs abbreviated notation with numerical arity \(n\) and argument list \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) or \(\bar{x}\), as well as the standard shorthand for quantified formulas: for a formula \(\varphi(a)\) with free variable \(a\) (and in general with variables \(a_1,\dots,a_n\)), the notation \(\forall x\,\varphi(x)\) (respectively \(\exists x\,\varphi(x)\), \(Q(x_1,\dots,x_n)\), \(F(\bar{x})\)) stands for the canonical formula \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) (respectively \(\exists x\,\varphi[x/a]\), \((Q(a_1,\dots,a_n))[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n]\), \((F(a_1,\dots,a_n))[\bar{x}/\bar{a}]\)). Expressions \(Q(x_1,\dots,x_n)\), \(F(\bar{x})\), \(\varphi(x)\) with bound variables are not themselves formulas or terms and are used solely within the scope of a matching quantifier prefix as shorthand expanded by the indicated substitutions. In general, when the specific arity of a symbol is not fixed, notation such as \(F(a,\dots,b)\), \(P(a,\dots,b)\) is used, or simply the head name \(F\) or \(P\) is written.

The construction of the set of all terms \(\Term\) broadly follows Definition 1.4, while adopting the idea of Remark 1.10, according to which one and the same term admits many different construction trees:

  1. Tm1.

    every free variable and every constant is a term;

  2. Tm2.

    if \(F(a,\dots,b)\) is a function symbol of signature \(\Lang\) written with pairwise distinct free variables \(a,\dots,b\), then \(F(a,\dots,b)\) is a term;

  3. Tm3.

    if \(R\) and \(T\) are terms and \(a\) is a free variable, then \(R[T/a]\) is a term;

  4. Tm4.

    no other terms exist.

The set of formulas \(\Form\) in signature \(\Lang\) is defined analogously:

  1. Fm1.

    if \(T,R\) are terms, then \((T = R)\) is a formula;

  2. Fm2.

    if \(P(a,\dots,b)\) is a predicate symbol of signature \(\Lang\) written with pairwise distinct free variables \(a,\dots,b\), then \(P(a,\dots,b)\) is a formula;

  3. Fm3.

    if \(\varphi\) is a formula, \(T\) is a term, and \(a\) is a free variable, then \(\varphi[T/a]\) is a formula;

  4. Fm4.

    if \(\varphi,\psi\) are formulas, then the following are also formulas: \[\neg\varphi,\;(\varphi\land\psi),\;(\varphi\lor\psi),\;(\varphi\to\psi),\; \forall x\;\varphi[x/a],\;\exists x\;\varphi[x/a],\] where \(a\) is an arbitrary free variable and the bound variable \(x\) does not occur in \(\varphi\);

  5. Fm5.

    no other formulas exist.

Formulas containing no connectives or quantifiers, i.e., equalities of terms or formulas obtained by substituting terms into predicate symbols (without applying rule Fm4), are called atomic.

A free variable occurs in a term or formula if it is a subword of that word. The quantifier \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) “closes” the variable \(a\): it does not occur in the resulting formula. A term or formula in which no free variable occurs is called closed; a closed formula is also called a sentence, and the class of sentences is denoted by \(\Sent\).

Because the classes \(\FVar\) and \(\BVar\) are disjoint, substituting a term \(T\) for a free variable \(a\) in a term \(R\) or formula \(\varphi\) coincides with word-for-word replacement \(R[T/a]\) and \(\varphi[T/a]\) and cannot cause variable capture by quantifiers. For the same reason, permitting rule Fm3 for arbitrary rather than only atomic formulas does not enlarge the class \(\Form\) (by Lemma 1.9, \(\Form\) is closed under substitutions \(\varphi[T/a]\)): the redundancy of rules Tm3 and Fm3 merely produces multiple construction trees for the same expression. For example, for a binary function symbol \(F(a,b)\), the term \(F(C,D)\) can be obtained from \(F(a,b)\) either in the order \((F(a,b)[C/a])[D/b]\) or in the order \((F(a,b)[D/b])[C/a]\) (as well as via any fresh intermediate variables or vacuous substitutions \(\xi[T/c]\) when \(c\) does not occur in \(\xi\)). Similarly, the formula \((P(C) \land P(D))\) is built either by rule Fm4 from the atomic formulas \(P(C)\) and \(P(D)\), or by rule Fm3 from \((P(a) \land P(b))\) via consecutive substitutions \([C/a]\) and \([D/b]\). Meanwhile, unique readability of every formula is preserved by Proposition 1.8.

2.2. Axioms and Rules of Inference

The predicate calculus is built over formulas of a fixed signature \(\Lang\) in Hilbert style: to the propositional axioms and Modus Ponens are added quantifier schemas, equality axioms, and quantifier introduction rules (Bernays' rules).

Definition 2.1 (The predicate “to be an axiom of FOL”). A word \(\xi\) has the property \(\Ax\) (written \(\Ax\mo \xi\mc\)) and is called an axiom of FOL if it is a formula and is identical to one of the following formulas (for arbitrary formulas \(\varphi, \psi, \chi\), propositional variables \(p, q, r\), free variable \(a\), bound variable \(x\), and terms \(T, R, T_0\)):

  1. Ax1.

    Propositional axiom schemas: \(\mathcal{A}[\varphi/p][\psi/q][\chi/r]\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is an axiom of PC (since \(\PVar\) and \(\Form\) are disjoint, replacements do not affect \(\varphi, \psi, \chi\), and the condition \(\xi \in \Form\) ensures that all propositional variables in \(\mathcal{A}\) have been replaced).

  2. Ax2.

    Quantifier axiom schemas (under the condition that the bound variable \(x\) does not occur in \(\varphi\); well-formedness \(\varphi[T/a] \in \Form\) is guaranteed by Lemma 1.9): \[\forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \varphi[T/a], \qquad \varphi[T/a] \to \exists x\,\varphi[x/a].\]

  3. Ax3.

    Equality axiom schemas:

    • reflexivity: \(T = T\);

    • congruence for terms: \((T = R) \to (T_0[T/a] = T_0[R/a])\);

    • congruence for formulas: \((T = R) \to (\varphi[T/a] \to \varphi[R/a])\).

No other words have the property \(\Ax\). All axioms of groups Ax1–Ax3 are logical: they are adopted for every signature and are not included in lists of non-logical axioms of specific theories. In predicate calculus without equality, group 3 is absent.

Remark 2.2 (Atomic form of the congruence axioms). In some expositions (for example, in formal arithmetic, where the axiom \(a = b \to S(a) = S(b)\) is written out for the successor operation \(S\)), congruence is postulated only for atomic expressions—the function and predicate symbols of the signature (and for equality itself)—after which the general schemas for arbitrary terms \(T_0\) and formulas \(\varphi\) are derived by structural induction, including induction on the number of arguments. The schemas of group 3 of Definition 2.1 are equivalent to such a specification and require no enumeration of signature symbols or their arities.

For a finite signature \(\Lang\), the class of axioms \(\Ax\) is decidable: for any word \(\xi\), parsing by Proposition 1.8 checks whether \(\xi\) is a formula, after which membership in the axioms is decided in finitely many steps. Specifically: for the propositional schemas Ax1 and reflexivity \((T = T)\), checking reduces to direct matching of subformulas and subterms along the parse tree (Proposition 1.8); for the quantifier schemas Ax2 (of the form \(\forall x\,\chi \to \theta\) or \(\theta \to \exists x\,\chi\)), the formula \(\varphi \equiv \chi[b/x]\) is recovered using the shortest variable \(b \in \FVar\) not occurring in \(\chi\), whereupon if \(b \notin \varphi\) one requires \(\theta \equiv \varphi\), and if \(b\) occurs in \(\varphi\) the term \(T\) is uniquely read off at the position of the first occurrence of \(b\); for the congruence schemas Ax3, the terms \(T, R\) are given by the antecedent \((T = R)\), while all candidate templates \(T_0\) or \(\varphi\) (with a single fresh variable \(a\)) correspond to the finitely many subsets of occurrences of \(T\) in the left-hand side of the consequent and are checked in finitely many steps.

Definition 2.3 (The predicate “to be a theorem of FOL”). The predicate \(\Thm\mo \xi\mc\) is defined recursively:

  1. T1.

    Basis: if \(\Ax\mo \varphi\mc\), then \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\).

  2. T2.

    Rule of Modus Ponens: if \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\) and \(\Thm\mo \q{\varphi \to \psi}\mc\), then \(\Thm\mo \psi\mc\).

  3. T3.

    Bernays' rules:

    • if \(\Thm\mo \q{\varphi \to \psi}\mc\), \(a\) does not occur in \(\varphi\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\psi\), then \(\Thm\mo \q{\varphi \to \forall x\,\psi[x/a]}\mc\);

    • if \(\Thm\mo \q{\varphi \to \psi}\mc\), \(a\) does not occur in \(\psi\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\varphi\), then \(\Thm\mo \q{\exists x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \psi}\mc\).

  4. T4.

    Closure: no other words have the property \(\Thm\).

A construction for the predicate \(\Thm\) is called a derivation (or proof) in FOL.

The mutual arrangement of the syntactic classes of a fixed signature \(\Lang\)—terms (\(\Term\)), bound variables (\(\BVar\)), and formulas (\(\Form\)), including sentences (\(\Sent\)), axioms (\(\Ax\)), and theorems (\(\Thm\))—is shown in Fig. 4.

Proposition 2.4 (Derived generalization rule). If \(\Thm\mo \psi\mc\), then \(\Thm\mo \q{\forall x\,\psi[x/a]}\mc\) for any free variable \(a\) and any bound variable \(x\) not occurring in \(\psi\).

Proof.

Choose a free variable \(b\) distinct from \(a\) and set \(\psi' \equiv \psi[b/a]\); then \(a\) does not occur in \(\psi'\). The formula \(\varphi \equiv \q{\psi' \to (\psi' \to \psi')}\) is a propositional axiom (obtained by substituting \([\psi'/p][\psi'/q]\) into \(p \to (q \to p)\)), so \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\) and \(a\) does not occur in \(\varphi\). By affirmation of the consequent \(\psi \to (\varphi \to \psi)\) and Modus Ponens, \(\Thm\mo \psi\mc\) implies \(\Thm\mo \q{\varphi \to \psi}\mc\). Since \(a\) does not occur in \(\varphi\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\psi\), Bernays' rule T3 yields \(\Thm\mo \q{\varphi \to \forall x\,\psi[x/a]}\mc\). Applying Modus Ponens to \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\) completes the derivation of \(\Thm\mo \q{\forall x\,\psi[x/a]}\mc\).∎

Every propositional tautology into which a substitution yields a formula of signature \(\Lang\) is derivable in FOL from group Ax1 and rule T2 alone (since the propositional part coincides with PC). For instance, \(\Thm\mo \q{\forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \exists x\,\varphi[x/a]}\mc\) (where \(x\) does not occur in \(\varphi\)) is derived from the two quantifier axioms \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \varphi\) and \(\varphi \to \exists x\,\varphi[x/a]\) (here \(T \equiv a\)) using the propositional theorem—the law of syllogism \(((\chi_1 \to \chi_2) \to ((\chi_2 \to \chi_3) \to (\chi_1 \to \chi_3)))\)—and two applications of rule T2 (Modus Ponens).

Example of a derivation tree. As an example of a complete derivation in FOL using exclusively rules T1–T3 without derived tautologies, consider the derivation tree of the theorem \(\exists y\,\forall x\,P(x, y) \to \forall x\,\exists y\,P(x, y)\) (for distinct \(a, b\) and distinct \(x, y\); Fig. 5). Unlike the derivation tree in the PC paper, it is oriented in the manner customary in logic: the axioms (leaves) stand at the top, and the theorem being proved (root) stands at the bottom.

Remark 2.5 (Undecidability of the class of theorems of FOL). Unlike the propositional calculus (where the class \(\Thm\) is decidable by truth tables), in the predicate calculus for a signature containing at least one binary predicate symbol (or a sufficient stock of function symbols), there exists no algorithm that determines in finitely many steps, for an arbitrary formula \(\varphi\), whether \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\) holds (the Church–Turing theorem). At the same time, the class \(\Thm\) itself remains recursively enumerable: an exhibited derivation is checked in finitely many steps.

2.3. Derivability in the Context of a List of Hypotheses

To formalize a derivation from a finite list of hypotheses as a single word, in § II.3 of the PC paper the base \(7\)-symbol alphabet was extended to \(\Alf'\) by a fresh separator symbol—the comma. In the first-order language, the comma already belongs to the \(16\)-symbol alphabet \(\Alf\) (inside terms and atomic formulas); nevertheless, by prefix-freeness of formulas (Lemma 1.7 (b)) and the editor property (§ I.1 of the PC paper), any external list of formulas \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k\) (as well as a sequence of formulas in a derivation) is uniquely parsed from left to right without introducing a \(17\)th separator symbol. Hereafter the comma is also used to write lists of hypotheses of the form \(\Gamma, \psi\) (for the empty context \(\Gamma\), the notation \(\Gamma, \psi\) stands for the single-element list \(\psi\)). Componentwise replacement \(\Gamma[b/a]\) in a list \(\Gamma\) is defined inductively: \(\psi[b/a]\) for a single-element list and \((\Gamma, \psi)[b/a] \equiv \Gamma[b/a], \psi[b/a]\) (for the empty context, \(\Gamma[b/a] \equiv \Gamma\)).

Definition 2.6 (List of formulas and derivability in a context). The predicate \(\List\mo \Gamma\mc\) and the relation \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\) (“formula \(\varphi\) occurs in list \(\Gamma\)”) are defined by simultaneous recursion:

  1. L1.

    Single-element list: \(\List\mo \psi\mc\) and \(\psi \trianglelefteq \psi\).

  2. L2.

    Appending a formula: if \(\List\mo \Gamma\mc\), then \(\List\mo \q{\Gamma,\psi}\mc\) and \(\psi \trianglelefteq \Gamma,\psi\); if moreover \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\), then \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma,\psi\).

  3. L3.

    Closure: no other lists and no other pairs of the relation \(\trianglelefteq\) exist.

As in PC, the metavariables \(\Gamma, \Delta\) range over lists of formulas and may also denote the empty context (in which no formula occurs). For a fixed context \(\Gamma\), the predicate \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\) (“formula \(\varphi\) is derivable in context \(\Gamma\)”) is defined recursively:

  1. D1.

    Axiom basis: if \(\Ax\mo \varphi\mc\), then \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\).

  2. D2.

    Hypothesis basis: if \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\), then \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\).

  3. D3.

    Modus Ponens: if \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\) and \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \psi\), then \(\Gamma \proves \psi\).

  4. D4.

    Bernays' rules in a context:

    • if \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \psi\), \(a\) occurs neither in any formula of \(\Gamma\) nor in \(\varphi\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\psi\), then \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \forall x\,\psi[x/a]\);

    • if \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \psi\), \(a\) occurs neither in any formula of \(\Gamma\) nor in \(\psi\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\varphi\), then \(\Gamma \proves \exists x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \psi\).

  5. D5.

    Closure: no other formulas are derivable in context \(\Gamma\).

The condition that \(a\) does not occur in the formulas of \(\Gamma\) in rule D4 is required to preserve semantic soundness: without it, from the hypothesis \(P(a)\) (that is, \(P(a) \proves (b = b) \to P(a)\)) one would derive \(\forall x\,P(x)\), even though property \(P\) for a single element does not entail that it holds for all elements. If \(a\) does not occur in \(\Gamma\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\psi\), then \(\Gamma \proves \psi\) yields \(\Gamma \proves \forall x\,\psi[x/a]\) by the same device as in Proposition 2.4.

Lemma 2.7 (Renaming of free variables in a derivation). Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a derivation of a formula \(\varphi\) in context \(\Gamma\) (\(\Gamma \proves \varphi\)), let \(a \in \FVar\) be an arbitrary free variable, and let the free variable \(b \in \FVar\) occur in no formula of \(\mathcal{D}\) (in particular, not in \(\Gamma\) or \(\varphi\)). Then \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \varphi[b/a]\), and there exists a derivation \(\mathcal{D}'\) of this statement whose length does not exceed the length of \(\mathcal{D}\).

Proof.

For \(b \equiv a\) the statement is trivial (\(\Gamma[a/a] \equiv \Gamma\), \(\varphi[a/a] \equiv \varphi\)). Assume \(b \not\equiv a\); proceed by induction on the number of steps (length) of the derivation \(\mathcal{D}\).

  • Axiom basis (D1): if \(\Ax\mo \varphi\mc\), then \(\Ax\mo \q{\varphi[b/a]}\mc\). Indeed:

    • for schema Ax1 (\(\varphi \equiv \mathcal{A}[\psi_1/p][\psi_2/q][\psi_3/r]\)), since \(\PVar\) and \(\FVar\) are disjoint, we have \(\varphi[b/a] \equiv \mathcal{A}[\psi_1[b/a]/p][\psi_2[b/a]/q][\psi_3[b/a]/r]\), where \(\psi_i[b/a] \in \Form\) by Lemma 1.9;

    • for schema Ax2 (\(\forall x\,\psi[x/c] \to \psi[T/c]\) or \(\psi[T/c] \to \exists x\,\psi[x/c]\) with \(x \notin \psi\)) and both congruence schemas Ax3 (\((T = R) \to (T_0[T/c] = T_0[R/c])\) and \((T = R) \to (\psi[T/c] \to \psi[R/c])\)) with parameter \(c \in \FVar\), note that if \(c \equiv a\), then \(a\) does not occur in \(\forall x\,\psi[x/a]\) (or \(\exists x\,\psi[x/a]\)), while \(b\) occurs neither in \(\psi\) nor in \(T_0\), whence \((\psi[T/a])[b/a] \equiv \psi[T[b/a]/a]\) and \((T_0[T/a])[b/a] \equiv T_0[T[b/a]/a]\) (and similarly for \(R\)), which by Lemma 1.9 again yields an axiom of the same schema. If instead \(c \not\equiv a\), then without loss of generality \(c \not\equiv a, b\): indeed, if \(c \equiv b\), it suffices to choose a fresh variable \(d \in \FVar\) occurring in none of \(T_0, \psi, T, R\) and distinct from \(a, b\), and rewrite the same axiom with parameter \(d\), since \(T_0[T/c] \equiv (T_0[d/c])[T/d]\), \(\psi[T/c] \equiv (\psi[d/c])[T/d]\) (and similarly for \(R\) and \([x/c]\)). When \(c \not\equiv a, b\), the word-for-word replacement \([b/a]\) commutes with \([x/c]\) and satisfies \((\psi[T/c])[b/a] \equiv (\psi[b/a])[T[b/a]/c]\), \((T_0[T/c])[b/a] \equiv (T_0[b/a])[T[b/a]/c]\) (and similarly for \(R\)); by Lemma 1.9, \(\psi[b/a] \in \Form\) (without \(x\)) and \(T_0[b/a], T[b/a], R[b/a] \in \Term\), so \(\varphi[b/a] \in \Ax\). Finally, \((T = T)[b/a] \equiv (T[b/a] = T[b/a]) \in \Ax\).

  • Hypothesis basis (D2): if \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\), then by the definition of componentwise replacement \(\varphi[b/a] \trianglelefteq \Gamma[b/a]\), whence \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \varphi[b/a]\).

  • Modus Ponens (D3): if the step passes from \(\chi\) and \(\chi \to \varphi\) to \(\varphi\), then by the induction hypothesis \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \chi[b/a]\) and \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \chi[b/a] \to \varphi[b/a]\), whence rule D3 yields \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \varphi[b/a]\).

  • Bernays' rules (D4): consider a step \(\Gamma \proves \chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/c]\) from the premise \(\Gamma \proves \chi_1 \to \chi_2\), where \(c\) does not occur in \(\Gamma\) or \(\chi_1\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_2\) (the second rule D4 is symmetric).

    • If \(c \equiv a\), then \(a\) occurs in none of \(\Gamma\), \(\chi_1\), and \(\forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]\). Consequently, \(\Gamma[b/a] \equiv \Gamma\) and \((\chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a])[b/a] \equiv \chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]\), so the original derivation \(\mathcal{D}\) itself supplies the required derivation.

    • If \(c \not\equiv a\) and \(c \not\equiv b\), then by the induction hypothesis applied to the subderivation of the premise, \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \chi_1[b/a] \to \chi_2[b/a]\). Since \(c \not\equiv b\) and \(c\) does not occur in \(\Gamma\) or \(\chi_1\), the variable \(c\) does not occur in \(\Gamma[b/a]\) or \(\chi_1[b/a]\); the variable \(x \in \BVar\) does not occur in \(\chi_2[b/a]\). Rule D4 gives \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \chi_1[b/a] \to \forall x\,(\chi_2[b/a])[x/c]\). Because \(c \not\equiv a, b\) and \(x \not\equiv a, b\), the replacements \([b/a]\) and \([x/c]\) commute: \((\chi_2[b/a])[x/c] \equiv (\chi_2[x/c])[b/a]\), which yields \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves (\chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/c])[b/a]\).

    • If \(c \equiv b\), then since \(b\) occurs in no formula of \(\mathcal{D}\), the variable \(b\) does not occur in \(\chi_2\), whence \(\chi_2[x/b] \equiv \chi_2\) and \((\chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/b])[b/a] \equiv \chi_1[b/a] \to \forall x\,\chi_2[b/a]\). By the induction hypothesis, \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \chi_1[b/a] \to \chi_2[b/a]\). Choosing a fresh variable \(e \in \FVar\) occurring in none of \(\Gamma[b/a]\), \(\chi_1[b/a]\), and \(\chi_2[b/a]\), and applying rule D4 (noting \((\chi_2[b/a])[x/e] \equiv \chi_2[b/a]\)), we obtain \(\Gamma[b/a] \proves \chi_1[b/a] \to \forall x\,\chi_2[b/a]\). ∎

Corollary 2.8 (\(\alpha\)-renaming of bound variables). For any formula \(\varphi \in \Form\), free variable \(a \in \FVar\), and bound variables \(x, y \in \BVar\) not occurring in \(\varphi\), the following equivalences are derivable in the calculus: \[\proves \forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \leftrightarrow \forall y\,\varphi[y/a], \qquad \proves \exists x\,\varphi[x/a] \leftrightarrow \exists y\,\varphi[y/a].\] In particular, for an arbitrary quantified formula \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi\) and a bound variable \(y \in \BVar\) not occurring in \(\chi\), one has \(\proves \mathsf{Q}x\,\chi \leftrightarrow \mathsf{Q}y\,\chi[y/x]\).

Proof.

By the quantifier axiom Ax2 (with \(T \equiv a\)), \(\proves \forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \varphi\). Since the free variable \(a\) does not occur in \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) and \(y\) does not occur in \(\varphi\), Bernays' rule T3 yields \(\proves \forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \forall y\,\varphi[y/a]\). Symmetrically, the converse implication \(\proves \forall y\,\varphi[y/a] \to \forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) is derivable. The case of \(\exists\) is dual (from \(\proves \varphi \to \exists y\,\varphi[y/a]\) by the second rule T3). The second statement follows by choosing a free variable \(b\) not occurring in \(\chi\): by Proposition 1.8 (b) and Lemma 1.9, the formula \(\varphi \equiv \chi[b/x]\) contains neither \(x\) nor \(y\), and satisfies \(\varphi[x/b] \equiv \chi\) and \(\varphi[y/b] \equiv \chi[y/x]\).∎

Definition 2.9 (\(\alpha\)-equivalence of formulas). The relation of \(\alpha\)-equivalence \(\varphi \approx \psi\) on \(\Form\) is defined as the least equivalence relation containing all pairs of the form \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi \approx \mathsf{Q}y\,\chi[y/x]\) (where \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi \in \Form\) and \(y \in \BVar\) does not occur in \(\chi\)) and closed under connectives (\(\varphi \approx \psi \implies \neg\varphi \approx \neg\psi\), \((\varphi \circ \chi) \approx (\psi \circ \chi)\), \((\chi \circ \varphi) \approx (\chi \circ \psi)\)) and the quantifier step (if \(\varphi \approx \psi\) and \(x \in \BVar\) occurs in neither \(\varphi\) nor \(\psi\), then \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\varphi[x/a] \approx \mathsf{Q}x\,\psi[x/a]\)).

Lemma 2.10 (Provable equivalence of \(\alpha\)-equivalent formulas). If \(\varphi \approx \psi\), then \(\proves \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\).

Proof.

Induction on the generation of \(\approx\): reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of \(\leftrightarrow\) follow from propositional tautologies, the basic pairs \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi \approx \mathsf{Q}y\,\chi[y/x]\) are derivable by Corollary 2.8, and preservation of provable equivalence under connectives and quantifiers is given by Proposition 2.13 (a).∎

Proposition 2.11 (Relation to the empty context).

  1. (a)

    \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\) if and only if \(\proves \varphi\).

  2. (b)

    If \(\Thm\mo \varphi\mc\), then \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\) for every context \(\Gamma\).

Proof.

Part (a) is immediate from the coincidence of rules T1–T3 with rules D1, D3, D4 when \(\Gamma\) is empty (in which no free variable occurs). Part (b) is a special case of monotonicity (Proposition 2.12 (a) with empty initial context, whose proof relies only on Lemma 2.7).∎

Proposition 2.12 (Monotonicity and the Deduction Theorem).

  1. (a)

    (Monotonicity in the context.) If \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\) and every formula occurring in \(\Gamma\) occurs in context \(\Delta\), then \(\Delta \proves \varphi\).

  2. (b)

    (Deduction Theorem.) \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \psi\) if and only if \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \psi\).

Proof.

(a) Proceed by induction on the length of the derivation \(\mathcal{D}\) of \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\). Steps D1–D3 transfer directly to context \(\Delta\) (in D2, \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\) entails \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Delta\) by hypothesis). Suppose the last step is rule D4: \(\Gamma \proves \chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]\) from a subderivation \(\mathcal{D}'\) of \(\Gamma \proves \chi_1 \to \chi_2\), where \(a\) does not occur in \(\Gamma\) or \(\chi_1\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_2\) (the second rule D4 is symmetric). Choose a free variable \(b \in \FVar\) occurring in no formula of the subderivation \(\mathcal{D}'\) or of the list \(\Delta\). By Lemma 2.7 applied to \(\mathcal{D}'\) with replacement \([b/a]\), since \(a\) does not occur in \(\Gamma\) or \(\chi_1\), we obtain a derivation of \(\Gamma \proves \chi_1 \to \chi_2[b/a]\) of length not exceeding that of \(\mathcal{D}'\). By the induction hypothesis, \(\Delta \proves \chi_1 \to \chi_2[b/a]\). Since \(b\) does not occur in \(\Delta\) or \(\chi_1\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_2[b/a]\), rule D4 in context \(\Delta\) yields \(\Delta \proves \chi_1 \to \forall x\,(\chi_2[b/a])[x/b]\). Because \(b\) does not occur in \(\chi_2\), we have \((\chi_2[b/a])[x/b] \equiv \chi_2[x/a]\), i.e., \(\Delta \proves \chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]\).

(b) The forward direction is proved by induction on the derivation of \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \psi\):

  • if \(\psi\) is an axiom or occurs in \(\Gamma\), then \(\Gamma \proves \psi\), and hence \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \psi\) (using \(\psi \to (\varphi \to \psi)\) and D3);

  • if \(\psi \equiv \varphi\), the propositional theorem \(\varphi \to \varphi\) is used;

  • a step D3 is handled by Frege's axiom;

  • if \(\psi \equiv \chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]\) is obtained by the first rule D4 from \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \chi_1 \to \chi_2\) under the conditions that \(a\) occurs in none of \(\Gamma\), \(\varphi\), and \(\chi_1\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_2\), then by the induction hypothesis \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to (\chi_1 \to \chi_2)\). Using the propositional tautology \((\varphi \to (\chi_1 \to \chi_2)) \to ((\varphi \land \chi_1) \to \chi_2)\), we obtain \(\Gamma \proves (\varphi \land \chi_1) \to \chi_2\). Since \(a\) occurs neither in \(\Gamma\) nor in \(\varphi \land \chi_1\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_2\), rule D4 in context \(\Gamma\) yields \(\Gamma \proves (\varphi \land \chi_1) \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]\), whence the propositional tautology \(((\varphi \land \chi_1) \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]) \to (\varphi \to (\chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a]))\) derives \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to (\chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a])\);

  • if \(\psi \equiv \exists x\,\chi_1[x/a] \to \chi_2\) is obtained by the second rule D4 from \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \chi_1 \to \chi_2\) under the conditions that \(a\) occurs in none of \(\Gamma\), \(\varphi\), and \(\chi_2\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_1\), then by the induction hypothesis \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to (\chi_1 \to \chi_2)\), whence a propositional tautology gives \(\Gamma \proves \chi_1 \to (\varphi \to \chi_2)\). Since \(a\) occurs neither in \(\Gamma\) nor in \(\varphi \to \chi_2\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi_1\), rule D4 in context \(\Gamma\) yields \(\Gamma \proves \exists x\,\chi_1[x/a] \to (\varphi \to \chi_2)\), and interchanging the antecedents completes the step.

The converse follows from part (a): if \(\Gamma \proves \varphi \to \psi\), then by part (a) \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \varphi \to \psi\), while by D2 \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \varphi\), whence D3 gives \(\Gamma, \varphi \proves \psi\).∎

Proposition 2.13 (Replacement of equivalent formulas and properties of equality).

  1. (a)

    If \(\proves \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\), then: \[\proves \neg\varphi \leftrightarrow \neg\psi,\qquad \proves (\varphi \circ \chi) \leftrightarrow (\psi \circ \chi),\qquad \proves (\chi \circ \varphi) \leftrightarrow (\chi \circ \psi),\] and for any free variable \(a\) and any bound variable \(x\) occurring in neither \(\varphi\) nor \(\psi\): \[\proves \forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \leftrightarrow \forall x\,\psi[x/a],\qquad \proves \exists x\,\varphi[x/a] \leftrightarrow \exists x\,\psi[x/a].\]

  2. (b)

    (Symmetry and transitivity of equality.) For any terms \(T, R, T_1, T_2, T_3 \in \Term\), the formulas \[(T = R) \to (R = T), \qquad (T_1 = T_2) \to ((T_2 = T_3) \to (T_1 = T_3))\] are derivable in the calculus.

Proof.

(a) For the propositional connectives, the claim follows by direct substitution of FOL formulas into the corresponding propositional theorems of PC (\((p \leftrightarrow q) \to (\neg p \leftrightarrow \neg q)\), \((p \leftrightarrow q) \to ((p \circ r) \leftrightarrow (q \circ r))\), and \((p \leftrightarrow q) \to ((r \circ p) \leftrightarrow (r \circ q))\)), which become theorems of FOL by group Ax1 and rule T2. For \(\forall\): from \(\proves \varphi \to \psi\) and the quantifier axiom \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \varphi\) (with \(T \equiv a\)) one obtains \(\proves \forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \psi\), whence by the first rule T3 (since \(a\) does not occur in \(\forall x\,\varphi[x/a]\) and \(x\) does not occur in \(\psi\)) it follows that \(\proves \forall x\,\varphi[x/a] \to \forall x\,\psi[x/a]\); the converse implication is derived symmetrically. For \(\exists\), the axiom \(\psi \to \exists x\,\psi[x/a]\) and the second rule T3 are used.

(b) For symmetry, choose a free variable \(a\) not occurring in \(T\) and apply the congruence schema for formulas to \(\varphi \equiv (a = T)\): this gives \((T = R) \to ((T = T) \to (R = T))\), which together with the axiom \(T = T\) yields \((T = R) \to (R = T)\). For transitivity, choose \(a\) not occurring in \(T_3\) and apply the same schema to \(\varphi \equiv (a = T_3)\) at the pair \((T_2, T_1)\): this gives \((T_2 = T_1) \to ((T_2 = T_3) \to (T_1 = T_3))\), which combined with symmetry \((T_1 = T_2) \to (T_2 = T_1)\) yields \((T_1 = T_2) \to ((T_2 = T_3) \to (T_1 = T_3))\).∎

2.4. First-Order Theories

Retaining the metavariables \(\Gamma, \Delta\) for finite lists of formulas (§ 2.3), we reserve upright uppercase letters \(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}\) for arbitrary (not necessarily finite) sets of formulas of signature \(\Lang\). For a set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\), one writes \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\) (or \(\mathrm{A} \proves_\Lang \varphi\) when the signature needs to be indicated explicitly) if there exists a finite list \(\Gamma\) of formulas from \(\mathrm{A}\) (possibly empty) such that \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\) in the sense of Definition 2.6.
