Because every derivation is finite, this relation is finitary, and by Proposition 2.12 it is monotonic in \(\mathrm{A}\) and satisfies the Deduction Theorem: \(\mathrm{A} \cup \{\varphi\} \proves \psi\) if and only if \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi \to \psi\).

Definition 2.14 (Deductive closure and consistency). Let \(\Lang\) be a fixed signature, and let \(\Sent_\Lang \subseteq \Form\) be the set of all sentences (closed formulas) of signature \(\Lang\).

  1. (a)

    The deductive closure of a set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) (in particular, of a set of sentences \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Sent_\Lang\)) in signature \(\Lang\) is the set of all sentences derivable from \(\mathrm{A}\): \[[\mathrm{A}]_\Lang \eqdef \{\varphi \in \Sent_\Lang \mid \mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\}.\]

  2. (b)

    A set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) is called consistent if there exists no formula \(\varphi \in \Form\) such that simultaneously \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\) and \(\mathrm{A} \proves \neg\varphi\) (when \(\Sent_\Lang \neq \emptyset\), by the propositional tautology \(p \to (\neg p \to q)\) this is equivalent to \([\mathrm{A}]_\Lang \neq \Sent_\Lang\); moreover, \(\Sent_\Lang \neq \emptyset\) both in FOL with equality, which contains \(\forall x\,(x = x)\), and in FOL without equality when \(\mathrm{Pred}_\Lang \neq \emptyset\), which contains \(\forall x\,P(x,\dots,x)\)), and inconsistent otherwise.

Because \([\mathrm{A}]_\Lang \subseteq \Sent_\Lang\) by definition, if \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) contains formulas with free variables, the inclusion \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq [\mathrm{A}]_\Lang\) fails (only \(\mathrm{A} \cap \Sent_\Lang \subseteq [\mathrm{A}]_\Lang\) holds). In model theory and axiomatic theories, one generally restricts attention to sets of sentences \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Sent_\Lang\): for these, \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq [\mathrm{A}]_\Lang\) and \([\mathrm{A}]_\Lang = [[\mathrm{A}]_\Lang]_\Lang\) always hold (the closure operation is idempotent).

Definition 2.15 (Theory and axiomatization).

  1. (a)

    A (first-order) theory in signature \(\Lang\) is a consistent, deductively closed set of sentences \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \Sent_\Lang\) (that is, \([\mathcal{T}]_\Lang = \mathcal{T}\) and \(\mathcal{T} \neq \Sent_\Lang\)). The elements of \(\mathcal{T}\) are called theorems of the theory \(\mathcal{T}\).

  2. (b)

    For a theory \(\mathcal{T}\), any subset \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \mathcal{T}\) satisfying \(\mathcal{T} = [\mathrm{A}]_\Lang\) is called an axiomatization (or axiom system) of \(\mathcal{T}\), and the elements of \(\mathrm{A}\) are called the non-logical axioms of that axiomatization. A theory \(\mathcal{T}\) is called finitely axiomatizable if it admits a finite axiomatization.

For an arbitrary set of sentences \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Sent_\Lang\), its deductive closure \([\mathrm{A}]_\Lang\) is a theory if and only if \(\mathrm{A}\) is consistent. Every theory \(\mathcal{T}\) is automatically non-empty, because deductive closure entails \([\emptyset]_\Lang \subseteq \mathcal{T}\): every logical theorem that is a sentence belongs to \(\mathcal{T}\). The consistency of \([\emptyset]_\Lang\) (which thus serves as the smallest theory by inclusion in signature \(\Lang\)) is established purely finitarily: define on \(\Form\) a valuation \(v(\varphi) \in \{0, 1\}\) by recursion on the number of connectives and quantifiers (justified by Proposition 1.8 and Lemma 1.9), erasing terms and quantifiers: set \(v(\varphi) = 1\) for every atomic formula, compute the connectives \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to\) by the truth tables on \(\{0, 1\}\), and for quantified formulas set \(v(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi) = v(\chi[b/x])\), where \(b \in \FVar\) is the shortest free variable not occurring in \(\chi\). By simultaneous induction on the number of connectives and quantifiers in \(\varphi\), two properties are verified: (1) for any quantified formula \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\chi\), the value \(v(\chi[c/x])\) does not depend on the choice of \(c \in \FVar\) not occurring in \(\chi\) (since \(\chi[c/x] \equiv (\chi[b/x])[c/b]\), the second property applies to the formula \(\chi[b/x]\) of smaller complexity), and (2) \(v(\varphi[T/a]) = v(\varphi)\) for all \(T \in \Term\) and \(a \in \FVar\) (for an atomic formula \(\varphi[T/a]\) remains atomic, connectives are preserved by the induction hypothesis, and for \(\mathsf{Q}y\,\chi\) choosing a fresh \(c \notin \chi, T, a\) gives \((\chi[T/a])[c/y] \equiv (\chi[c/y])[T/a]\), whence by the induction hypothesis and property (1), \(v((\mathsf{Q}y\,\chi)[T/a]) = v((\chi[c/y])[T/a]) = v(\chi[c/y]) = v(\mathsf{Q}y\,\chi)\)). In particular, for the quantifier axioms Ax2, \(v(\forall x\,\psi[x/a]) = v(\psi) = v(\psi[T/a])\) (and similarly for \(\exists\)), so every axiom of groups Ax1–Ax3 receives the value \(1\), and rules T2–T3 preserve the value \(1\). Consequently, \(v(\theta) = 1\) for all \(\theta\) with \(\Thm\mo \theta\mc\), whereas \(v(\neg\theta) = 0\) (in particular, for any formula \(\varphi \in \Form\), \(v(\varphi \to \varphi) = 1\) and \(v(\neg(\varphi \to \varphi)) = 0\), so \(\neg(\varphi \to \varphi)\) is not derivable).

Separating the non-logical axioms from the theory itself as a generating set highlights that one and the same theory admits different axiomatizations; independence of axioms (the requirement that no axiom \(\alpha \in \mathrm{A}\) be derivable from \(\mathrm{A} \setminus \{\alpha\}\)) is not required in the definition of an axiomatization, which simplifies comparing different axiom systems and theories (in particular, \(\mathcal{T}\) itself serves as its own axiomatization). If \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Sent_\Lang\) and a formula \(\varphi \in \Form\) contains free variables \(a_1, \dots, a_k\), then by the generalization rule (Proposition 2.4) and the \(\forall\)-elimination axiom, derivability \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\) is equivalent to derivability of its universal closure \(\mathrm{A} \proves \forall x_1 \dots \forall x_k\,\varphi[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_k/a_k]\). For this reason, an open formula in non-logical axioms is frequently written as standard shorthand for its universal closure.

Definition 2.16 (Deductively complete theory). A theory \(\mathcal{T}\) in signature \(\Lang\) is called deductively complete (or simply complete) if for every sentence \(\varphi \in \Sent_\Lang\), either \(\varphi \in \mathcal{T}\) or \(\neg\varphi \in \mathcal{T}\).

Example 2.17 (Examples of first-order theories).

  1. (1)

    Pure equality and cardinality axioms. In the empty signature \(\Lang = \emptyset\), the sole atomic predicate is equality \(=\). For each \(n \ge 2\), the sentence \[\alpha_{\ge n} \eqdef \exists x_1 \dots \exists x_n \bigwedge_{1 \le i < j \le n} \neg(x_i = x_j)\] expresses the existence of at least \(n\) distinct elements, while \(\beta_{=n} \eqdef \alpha_{\ge n} \land \neg\alpha_{\ge n+1}\) (for \(n = 1\): \(\beta_{=1} \eqdef \neg\alpha_{\ge 2}\)) expresses the existence of exactly \(n\) elements. Each singleton set \(\{\beta_{=n}\}\) (\(n \ge 1\)), as well as the set \(\{\alpha_{\ge n} \mid n \ge 2\}\), is consistent, and the theories they generate—\([\{\beta_{=n}\}]_\emptyset\) and \(\mathrm{Th}_\infty \eqdef [\{\alpha_{\ge n} \mid n \ge 2\}]_\emptyset\) (the theory of infinite sets)—are deductively complete (by quantifier elimination, every sentence in \(\Lang = \emptyset\) reduces to a Boolean combination of the sentences \(\alpha_{\ge k}\); see, e.g., Chang and Keisler, 1990; Shoenfield, 1967), whereas pure logic of equality \([\emptyset]_\emptyset\) is incomplete (neither \(\alpha_{\ge 2}\) nor \(\neg\alpha_{\ge 2}\) is derivable in it). Moreover, \(\mathrm{Th}_\infty\) is not finitely axiomatizable (by the Compactness Theorem, obtained below in Section 3, Remark 3.6).

  2. (2)

    Dense linear order without endpoints (\(\mathsf{DLO}\)). The signature \(\Lang = \{<\}\) consists of a single binary predicate symbol (written infix). The axioms are six sentences: irreflexivity \(\forall x\,\neg(x < x)\), transitivity \(\forall x\forall y\forall z\,((x < y \land y < z) \to x < z)\), linearity \(\forall x\forall y\,(x < y \lor x = y \lor y < x)\), density \(\forall x\forall y\,(x < y \to \exists z\,(x < z \land z < y))\), and the absence of least and greatest elements \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(y < x)\), \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x < y)\). This axiom system is consistent, and the theory \(\mathsf{DLO}\) it generates is finitely axiomatizable and deductively complete (Chang and Keisler, 1990).

  3. (3)

    Torsion-free abelian groups. In the signature \(\Lang = \{+, 0\}\) (a binary function symbol and a constant), to the abelian group axioms \[\begin{gather*} \forall x\forall y\forall z\,((x + y) + z = x + (y + z)), \qquad \forall x\,(x + 0 = x), \\ \forall x\,\exists y\,(x + y = 0), \qquad \forall x\forall y\,(x + y = y + x) \end{gather*}\] is added the infinite family of torsion-free axioms \(\forall x\,(n \cdot x = 0 \to x = 0)\) for all \(n \ge 2\), where \(n \cdot T\) denotes the \(n\)-fold sum \(T + \dots + T\). This theory is incomplete (the sentence \(\exists x\,\neg(x = 0)\) is independent of it); however, adjoining the nontriviality axiom \(\exists x\,\neg(x = 0)\) and the divisibility schema \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(n \cdot y = x)\) (\(n \ge 2\)) yields the complete theory of nontrivial divisible torsion-free abelian groups (Chang and Keisler, 1990; Shoenfield, 1967).

  4. (4)

    Axiomatic set theory (\(\mathsf{ZFC}\)). The signature \(\Lang = \{\in\}\) contains a single binary membership predicate symbol and neither constants nor function symbols. The system of non-logical axioms of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) comprises the axioms of extensionality, pairing, union, power set, infinity, regularity (foundation), the axiom of choice, and the axiom schemas of separation and replacement; assuming consistency (\(\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\)), the closure of this axiom system is a theory in the sense of Definition 2.15. The only terms of the language \(\mathrm{Term}_{\{\in\}}\) are free variables, so the standard notation \(\emptyset\), \(\{a, b\}\), \(\mathcal{P}(a)\), \(a \subseteq b\) does not formally belong to the base signature and is introduced via definitional extensions.

2.5. Definitional Extensions of the Language and Theories

Developing substantive theories in a minimal signature (such as \(\{\in\}\) in set theory or \(\{0, S, +, \cdot\}\) in arithmetic) requires introducing new symbols—predicates, functions, and constants—as abbreviations for expressions of the original language. While a new predicate symbol is always specified by a formula, introducing a function symbol or constant requires that the defining condition uniquely determine an element in the theory.

To abbreviate notation, the unique existence quantifier is used: for a formula \(\varphi \in \Form\), a free variable \(a\), and distinct bound variables \(x, y \in \BVar\) not occurring in \(\varphi\), one sets \[\exists! x\,\varphi[x/a] \eqdef \exists x\,\bigl(\varphi[x/a] \land \forall y\,(\varphi[y/a] \to y = x)\bigr).\]

Definition 2.18 (Definitional extension). Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a theory in signature \(\Lang\), and let \(\Lang' = \Lang \cup \{S\}\) be the extension of the signature by a fresh non-logical symbol \(S\) (a constant or template) whose head name does not occur in \(\Lang\) (so \(\Lang'\) preserves the antichain property, Definition 1.3). A definitional extension of \(\mathcal{T}\) by the symbol \(S\) is the theory \(\mathcal{T}' = [\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_S\}]_{\Lang'}\) in signature \(\Lang'\), where the defining axiom \(\alpha_S \in \Sent_{\Lang'}\) has one of the following three forms (depending on the kind of symbol \(S\), with the bound variables \(x_1, \dots, x_n, y \in \BVar\) pairwise distinct and not occurring in the defining formula \(\chi \in \Form\)):

  1. (1)

    Introducing a predicate symbol \(Q(a_1, \dots, a_n)\): for an arbitrary formula \(\chi \in \Form\) in which no free variables other than \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) occur, one sets \[\alpha_Q \equiv \forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,\bigl(Q(x_1, \dots, x_n) \leftrightarrow \chi[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n]\bigr).\]

  2. (2)

    Introducing a function symbol \(F(a_1, \dots, a_n)\) (\(n \ge 1\)): let \(\chi \in \Form\) be a formula all of whose free variables are among \(a_1, \dots, a_n, b\), such that the existence and uniqueness condition is derivable in \(\mathcal{T}\): \[\forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,\exists! y\,\chi[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n][y/b] \in \mathcal{T}.\] Then one sets \[\alpha_F \equiv \forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n \forall y\,\bigl(F(x_1, \dots, x_n) = y \leftrightarrow \chi[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n][y/b]\bigr).\] Because \(\forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,\exists! y\,\chi[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n][y/b] \in \mathcal{T}\), this axiom is deductively equivalent to the sentence \(\beta_F \equiv \forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,\chi[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n][F(x_1, \dots, x_n)/b]\).

  3. (3)

    Introducing a constant \(C\): the special case of (2) for \(n = 0\). If all free variables of \(\chi \in \Form\) are among \(b\) (i.e., either only \(b\) or none) and \(\exists! y\,\chi[y/b] \in \mathcal{T}\), then \[\alpha_C \equiv \forall y\,\bigl(C = y \leftrightarrow \chi[y/b]\bigr),\] which over \(\mathcal{T}\) is equivalent to the sentence \(\beta_C \equiv \chi[C/b]\).

An iterated definitional extension is the union of a finite or countable ascending chain of theories \(\mathcal{T}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \dots\) in which each step \(\mathcal{T}_{k+1}\) is a definitional extension of \(\mathcal{T}_k\).

Remark 2.19 (Explicit term abbreviations and propagation of congruence). A frequent source of new function symbols and constants is an explicit term abbreviation: let \(T \in \Term\) contain only free variables from \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) (\(n \ge 0\)), and suppose a symbol \(F(a_1, \dots, a_n)\) (or a constant \(C\) for \(n = 0\)) is introduced as an abbreviation for \(T\). This case falls under clause (2) of Definition 2.18 with \(\chi \equiv (b = T)\) (where \(b\) does not occur in \(T\)): the condition \(\forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,\exists! y\,(y = T[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n])\) is derivable purely logically (for the empty theory \([\emptyset]_\Lang\)) from reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of equality, and the axiom \(\alpha_F\) is equivalent to \[\beta_F \equiv \forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,\bigl(F(x_1, \dots, x_n) = T[x_1/a_1]\dots[x_n/a_n]\bigr).\] Adding the new symbol \(S\) to the signature \(\Lang'\) immediately expands the classes \(\mathrm{Term}_{\Lang'}\) and \(\mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\): in particular, \(F\) may appear inside compound terms at arbitrary depth and in the arguments of arbitrary predicates. For such an abbreviation to genuinely permit substituting \(F\) for \(T\) (and vice versa) in any context, congruence of equality must extend to the new symbol. In the formulation of the predicate calculus adopted in Definition 2.1, the congruence schemas Ax3 apply to all terms and formulas of the current signature, so upon passing from \(\Lang\) to \(\Lang'\) the axioms \[(R_1 = R'_1 \land \dots \land R_n = R'_n) \to \bigl(F(R_1, \dots, R_n) = F(R'_1, \dots, R'_n)\bigr)\] immediately belong to the logical axioms of \(\Lang'\) (in the atomic formulation of Remark 2.2, the same implication follows from congruence for \(T\), and in the general case of Definition 2.18 (2) from congruence for \(\chi\) and uniqueness). Together with schema Ax3 for formulas \(\varphi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\), the defining axiom \(\alpha_F\) entails \[\mathcal{T}' \proves_{\Lang'} \varphi[F(R_1, \dots, R_n)/c] \leftrightarrow \varphi[T[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n]/c]\] for any terms \(R_1, \dots, R_n \in \mathrm{Term}_{\Lang'}\) and free variable \(c\), so the new notation and the term it abbreviates are interchangeable in every formula of the extended language.

The next theorem shows that a definitional extension not only allows every formula of the extended language to be translated back into the base language \(\Lang\), but also generates no new theorems in the old language.

Theorem 2.20 (Eliminability and conservativity of definitional extensions). Let \(\mathcal{T}' = [\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_S\}]_{\Lang'}\) be a definitional extension of a theory \(\mathcal{T}\) in signature \(\Lang\) (Definition 2.18), and let \(\FV(\psi)\) denote the set of all free variables occurring in a formula \(\psi\). There exists a constructive map \(\varphi \mapsto \varphi^*\) from \(\mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\) to \(\Form\) that introduces no new free variables (\(\FV(\varphi^*) \subseteq \FV(\varphi)\)) and satisfies the following properties:

  1. (a)

    \(\varphi^* \equiv \varphi\) for every formula \(\varphi \in \Form\);

  2. (b)

    \(\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_S\} \proves_{\Lang'} \varphi \leftrightarrow \varphi^*\) for every formula \(\varphi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\);

  3. (c)

    (syntactic conservativity) for every sentence \(\varphi \in \Sent_\Lang\), \[\varphi \in \mathcal{T}' \iff \varphi \in \mathcal{T}.\]

Proof.

First specify a canonical translation \(\varphi \mapsto \varphi^* \in \Form\). Given a formula \(\varphi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\), rename the bound variables in the defining formula \(\chi\) (inside \(\alpha_S\)) to the shortest variables in \(\BVar\) not occurring in \(\varphi\): by Lemma 2.10, this leaves \(\chi\) unchanged up to provable equivalence. Next, \(\psi^*\) for subformulas \(\psi\) of \(\varphi\) is defined by recursion on the construction of \(\psi\) (with the renamed formula \(\chi\) fixed, and in the function case choosing the shortest fresh variable \(y \in \BVar\) not occurring in \(\varphi\), \(\chi\), or the already translated portion):

  • If \(S\) is a predicate symbol \(Q\), then on an atomic formula we set \(Q(R_1, \dots, R_n)^* \equiv \chi[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n]\) (here \(R_i \in \Term\)), and leave all other atomic formulas unchanged.

  • If \(S\) is a function symbol \(F\) (or a constant \(C\), treated as the case \(n = 0\)), then every atomic formula \(\psi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\) containing \(F\) has at least one innermost occurrence \(F(R_1, \dots, R_n)\) (where \(R_1, \dots, R_n \in \Term\) do not contain \(F\)). Choosing the first such occurrence, write \(\psi \equiv \psi_0[F(R_1, \dots, R_n)/c]\) for the shortest free variable \(c\) occurring in neither \(\psi\) nor \(\chi\) and the shortest bound variable \(y \in \BVar\) occurring in none of \(\varphi\), \(\chi\), and \(\psi_0^*\), and replace \(\psi\) by the formula \[\exists y\,\bigl(\chi[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n][y/b] \land \psi_0^*[y/c]\bigr),\] in which \(\psi_0\) contains one fewer occurrence of \(F\) (so the recursion on the number of occurrences of \(F\) in an atomic formula terminates; when \(F\) does not occur in an atom \(\psi\), set \(\psi^* \equiv \psi\)). In the special case of an explicit term abbreviation \(F(a_1, \dots, a_n) = T\) (Remark 2.19), this step amounts to direct word-for-word replacement of \(F(R_1, \dots, R_n)\) by \(T[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n]\) inside the terms of the atomic formula.

  • To connectives and quantifiers, the translation extends canonically (independently of the choice of representation of the quantified formula): \[(\neg\psi)^* \equiv \neg(\psi^*),\qquad (\psi_1 \circ \psi_2)^* \equiv (\psi_1^* \circ \psi_2^*),\qquad (\mathsf{Q}x\,\psi)^* \equiv \mathsf{Q}x\,\bigl((\psi[b/x])^*\bigr)[x/b],\] where \(b \in \FVar\) is the shortest free variable not occurring in \(\psi\) (by Proposition 1.8 (b) and Lemma 1.9, \(\psi[b/x] \in \Form\) has strictly smaller complexity; since all newly introduced bound variables from \(\chi\) and \(y\) are chosen outside \(\varphi\), and hence distinct from \(x\), the variable \(x\) does not occur in \((\psi[b/x])^*\)).

Because the choice of fresh bound variables in \(\chi\) and \(y\) depends on the entire formula \(\varphi\) being translated, for subformulas \(\psi_1, \psi_2\) of a single formula \(\varphi\), their standalone translations may differ from their translations inside \(\varphi\) only by renaming of fresh bound variables. Thus, by induction and Definition 2.9, the translation respects connectives, quantifiers, and replacement of free variables up to \(\alpha\)-equivalence (\(\approx\)): \((\neg\psi)^* \approx \neg(\psi^*)\), \((\psi_1 \circ \psi_2)^* \approx (\psi_1^* \circ \psi_2^*)\), \((\mathsf{Q}x\,\psi_0[x/a])^* \approx \mathsf{Q}x\,(\psi_0^*)[x/a]\), and \((\psi[b/a])^* \approx (\psi^*)[b/a]\) (in the quantifier identity, when \(b \notin \psi_0[x/a]\), we have \(b \notin \psi_0^*\) since \(\FV(\psi_0^*) \subseteq \FV(\psi_0)\), whence \(((\psi_0^*)[b/a])[x/b] \equiv (\psi_0^*)[x/a]\)). Up to \(\approx\), the translation does not depend on the choice of fresh variables.

Claim (a) is immediate from the construction: formulas in \(\Form\) do not contain \(S\). The inclusion \(\FV(\varphi^*) \subseteq \FV(\varphi)\) follows because \(\chi\) contains only free variables from \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) (together with \(b\), which is bound by \(\exists y\)), and the substituted terms \(R_i\) contain only variables from \(\varphi\). Equality \(\FV(\varphi^*) = \FV(\varphi)\) does not hold in general: for instance, if \(\chi \equiv \forall z\,(z = z)\), then \(Q(a)^* \equiv \forall z\,(z = z)\) no longer contains \(a\).

Claim (b) is checked by induction on the construction of \(\varphi\) (in the function case, with a nested induction on the number of occurrences of \(F\) in an atomic formula). For an atomic formula \(Q(R_1, \dots, R_n)\), the equivalence \(Q(R_1, \dots, R_n) \leftrightarrow \chi[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n]\) is obtained by substituting the terms \(R_1, \dots, R_n\) into the axiom \(\alpha_Q\) (via the \(\forall\)-elimination schema). For an atomic formula \(\psi \equiv \psi_0[F(R_1, \dots, R_n)/c]\), the axiom \(\alpha_F\) yields the equivalence \[\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_F\} \proves_{\Lang'} \forall y\,\bigl(F(R_1, \dots, R_n) = y \leftrightarrow \chi[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n][y/b]\bigr).\] From reflexivity \(F(R_1, \dots, R_n) = F(R_1, \dots, R_n)\) and this equivalence, one derives \(\psi \to \exists y\,(\chi[R_1/a_1]\dots[R_n/a_n][y/b] \land \psi_0[y/c])\); conversely, \(\chi[\bar{R}/\bar{a}][y/b] \land \psi_0[y/c]\) implies \(F(\bar{R}) = y\), whence the congruence schema Ax3 for formulas derives \(\psi_0[F(\bar{R})/c] \equiv \psi\). Replacing \(\psi_0\) by \(\psi_0^*\) is justified by the nested induction hypothesis, Proposition 2.13 (a), and Lemma 2.10; by the same results, the inductive step for connectives and quantifiers preserves equivalence (passing from \(\neg(\psi_1^*)\), \(\psi_1^* \circ \psi_2^*\), \(\mathsf{Q}x\,(\psi_0^*)[x/a]\) to \((\neg\psi_1)^*\), \((\psi_1 \circ \psi_2)^*\), \((\mathsf{Q}x\,\psi_0[x/a])^*\) via Lemma 2.10).

To prove (c), it suffices to show that \(\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_S\} \proves_{\Lang'} \psi\) implies \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \psi^*\) for every formula \(\psi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\) (then for \(\varphi \in \Sent_\Lang\), property (a) gives \(\varphi^* \equiv \varphi\), whence \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \varphi\), i.e., \(\varphi \in \mathcal{T}\)). Proceed by induction on the derivation from \(\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_S\}\) in \(\Lang'\):

  • Hypotheses and axiom \(\alpha_S\). If \(\psi \in \mathcal{T}\), then \(\psi^* \equiv \psi \in \mathcal{T}\). For \(\psi \equiv \alpha_Q\), the formula \(\alpha_Q^* \approx \forall x_1 \dots \forall x_n\,(\chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}] \leftrightarrow \chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}])\) is a logical theorem (by Lemma 2.10). For \(\psi \equiv \alpha_F\), the translation \((F(\bar{x}) = y)^*\) is equivalent in \(\mathcal{T}\) to \(\chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}][y/b]\) (by \(\forall \bar{x}\,\exists! z\,\chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}][z/b] \in \mathcal{T}\): specifically, \(\exists z\,(\chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}][z/b] \land z = y) \leftrightarrow \chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}][y/b]\)), so \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \alpha_F^*\).

  • Rules of inference. If \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \psi_1^*\) and \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang (\psi_1 \to \psi_2)^*\), then since \((\psi_1 \to \psi_2)^* \approx (\psi_1^* \to \psi_2^*)\) and by Lemma 2.10, we have \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \psi_1^* \to \psi_2^*\), whence Modus Ponens yields \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \psi_2^*\). Bernays' rules (respecting the side condition on free variables) are also preserved: from \(\FV(\psi^*) \subseteq \FV(\psi)\) it follows that non-occurrence of the free variable \(a\) is preserved by translation, and the relations \((\chi_1 \to \chi_2)^* \approx (\chi_1^* \to \chi_2^*)\) and \((\chi_1 \to \forall x\,\chi_2[x/a])^* \approx \chi_1^* \to \forall x\,(\chi_2^*)[x/a]\) (and similarly for \(\exists\); renaming \(x\) in \(\chi_1^*\), \(\chi_2^*\) via Lemma 2.10 if needed should it occur among the fresh variables of the translation) allow applying Bernays' rule and returning to the translation of the conclusion via Lemma 2.10.

  • Logical axioms. For a propositional axiom \(\mathcal{A}[\psi_1/p][\psi_2/q][\psi_3/r]\), its translation is \(\alpha\)-equivalent to the axiom \(\mathcal{A}[\psi_1^*/p][\psi_2^*/q][\psi_3^*/r]\) and is therefore derivable in \(\mathcal{T}\) by Lemma 2.10. In the predicate case \(S = Q\), we have \(\mathrm{Term}_{\Lang'} = \Term\), and induction on the complexity of \(\psi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\) verifies \((\psi[T/a])^* \approx \psi^*[T/a]\) for all \(T \in \Term\) and \(a \in \FVar\), whence translations of axioms Ax2 and Ax3 are \(\alpha\)-equivalent to axioms of the same schemas in \(\Lang\) and derivable by Lemma 2.10. In the function case \(S = F\) (or constant \(C\) for \(n = 0\)), choose a fresh free variable \(d \in \FVar\) occurring in none of \(T, R, T_0, \psi, \chi\) and distinct from \(a_1, \dots, a_n, b\), together with fresh bound variables \(z_1, \dots, z_n, y \in \BVar\), and assign to each term \(T \in \mathrm{Term}_{\Lang'}\) a formula \(\varphi_T(d) \in \Form\) expressing the equality \(d = T\): for \(T \in \Term\) set \(\varphi_T(d) \equiv (d = T)\), and for a compound term \(F(R_1, \dots, R_n)\) set \[\varphi_{F(R_1, \dots, R_n)}(d) \equiv \exists z_1 \dots \exists z_n\,\bigl(\varphi_{R_1}[z_1/d] \land \dots \land \varphi_{R_n}[z_n/d] \land \chi[z_1/a_1]\dots[z_n/a_n][d/b]\bigr)\] (for \(n = 0\) and a constant \(C\), set \(\varphi_C(d) \equiv \chi[d/b]\)). The verification then splits into three steps:

    1. 1)

      By structural induction on \(T \in \mathrm{Term}_{\Lang'}\), from \(\forall \bar{x}\,\exists! y\,\chi[\bar{x}/\bar{a}][y/b] \in \mathcal{T}\) and congruence of equality in \(\Lang\) one derives \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \exists! y\,\varphi_T[y/d]\).

    2. 2)

      Because \(\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang \exists! y\,\varphi_T[y/d]\), the formula \(\exists y\,(\varphi_T[y/d] \land \theta[y/a])\) is equivalent in \(\mathcal{T}\) to \(\forall y\,(\varphi_T[y/d] \to \theta[y/a])\) and hence commutes in \(\mathcal{T}\) with all connectives \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to\) and quantifiers \(\forall, \exists\). Combined with the nested induction on the number of occurrences of \(F\) for atomic formulas (where uniqueness \(\exists! z\,\varphi_R[z/d]\) allows witnesses for different occurrences of \(a\) to be identified), induction on the complexity of \(\psi \in \mathrm{Form}_{\Lang'}\) gives the equivalence \[\mathcal{T} \proves_\Lang (\psi[T/a])^* \leftrightarrow \exists y\,\bigl(\varphi_T[y/d] \land \psi^*[y/a]\bigr)\] (for \(y \in \BVar\) occurring in neither \(\psi^*\) nor \(\varphi_T\)).

    3. 3)

      From (1) and (2) follow the translations of all schemas Ax2 and Ax3: \((T = T)^*\) is equivalent in \(\mathcal{T}\) to \(\exists y_1 \exists y_2\,(\varphi_T[y_1/d] \land \varphi_T[y_2/d] \land y_1 = y_2)\), which holds under \(\exists! y\,\varphi_T[y/d]\); the translation \((T = R)^*\) is equivalent in \(\mathcal{T}\) to \(\exists y\,(\varphi_T[y/d] \land \varphi_R[y/d])\), which by uniqueness for \(\varphi_T\) and \(\varphi_R\) entails \(\forall y\,(\varphi_T[y/d] \leftrightarrow \varphi_R[y/d])\), and together with (2) yields the congruence schema for formulas (and as its special case for \(\psi \equiv (a_0 = T_0[R/a])\) with replacement \([T_0[T/a]/a_0]\), the congruence schema for terms); finally, for Ax2, from \((\forall x\,\psi[x/a])^* \approx \forall x\,(\psi^*)[x/a]\), the quantifier axiom in \(\Lang\), and \(\exists y\,\varphi_T[y/d]\) follows \(\exists y\,(\varphi_T[y/d] \land \psi^*[y/a])\), i.e., \((\psi[T/a])^*\) by (2) (the \(\exists\) case is dual).

The converse implication in (c) is immediate from the inclusion \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{T}'\).∎

By Theorem 2.20 and a straightforward induction on the number of steps, any iterated definitional extension is likewise conservative over the base theory \(\mathcal{T}\) (in particular, consistency of \(\mathcal{T}\) implies consistency of \(\mathcal{T} \cup \{\alpha_S\}\), so \(\mathcal{T}'\) is indeed a theory in signature \(\Lang'\)).

Example 2.21 (Definitional extensions in set theory). In the signature \(\Lang = \{\in\}\) of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) (Example 2.17 (4)), standard set-theoretic notation is introduced by a chain of definitional extensions:

  1. (1)

    The inclusion predicate \(a \subseteq b\) is defined unconditionally by the formula \(\chi_\subseteq \equiv \forall z\,(z \in a \to z \in b)\) with the axiom \(\forall x\forall y\,(x \subseteq y \leftrightarrow \forall z\,(z \in x \to z \in y))\).

  2. (2)

    The empty set constant \(\emptyset\) is defined by \(\chi_\emptyset \equiv \forall z\,\neg(z \in b)\): existence follows from the axioms of separation and infinity (or empty set existence), and uniqueness follows from the axiom of extensionality.

  3. (3)

    The binary function symbol for the unordered pair \(\{a_1, a_2\}\) is defined by \(\chi_{\{\cdot,\cdot\}} \equiv \forall z\,(z \in b \leftrightarrow (z = a_1 \lor z = a_2))\), whose existence and uniqueness are ensured by the pairing axiom and the axiom of extensionality.

  4. (4)

    The unary function symbol for the power set \(\mathcal{P}(a)\) is defined in the already extended language \(\{\in, \subseteq\}\) by \(\chi_{\mathcal{P}} \equiv \forall z\,(z \in b \leftrightarrow z \subseteq a)\) (on the basis of the power set axiom and extensionality).

  5. (5)

    A constant or function as an explicit term abbreviation: the singleton \(\{a\}\) is introduced as an abbreviation for \(\{a, a\}\), and the Kuratowski ordered pair \(\tuple{a_1, a_2}\) as an abbreviation for \(\{\{a_1\}, \{a_1, a_2\}\}\) following Remark 2.19.

Remark 2.22 (Hexadecimal coding of syntax and the path to Gödel's incompleteness theorems). Fixing in § 1.1 a single \(16\)-symbol object alphabet \(\Alf\) for all first-order signatures yields a direct arithmetization of syntax without appealing to prime factorization. Because external lists of hypotheses and finite derivations are written with commas inside the same alphabet \(\Alf\) (§ 2.3), assigning the hexadecimal digits \(0, 1, \dots, \mathrm{F}\) to the symbols of \(\Alf\) encodes every word \(\xi\) over \(\Alf\) (including terms, formulas, hypothesis lists, and derivations) bijectively as a natural number \(\ulcorner \xi \urcorner\) whose hexadecimal expansion is obtained by prepending a leading \(1\) to the digit string of \(\xi\) (the leading \(1\) prevents the loss of leading zeros). Under this coding, the basic operations of the special metalanguage of Part I of the PC paper—concatenation, subword occurrence testing, and word-for-word replacement \(\xi[\zeta/\eta]\)—are expressed by primitive recursive (indeed, Kalmar elementary) operations on base-\(16\) codes; for a decidable signature \(\Lang\), the syntactic predicates \(\Term\), \(\Form\), \(\Ax\) become primitive recursive relations on \(\N\), and for a decidable (respectively recursively enumerable) axiomatization \(\mathrm{A}\), the relation “\(d\) is the code of a derivation from \(\mathrm{A}\) of the formula with code \(n\)” is primitive recursive (respectively \(\Sigma_1\)), so the provability predicate \(\mathrm{Prov}_{\mathrm{A}}(n)\) is expressed by an arithmetic \(\Sigma_1\)-formula.

Both of Gödel's incompleteness theorems follow from this arithmetization for any consistent theory \(\mathcal{T} = [\mathrm{A}]_\Lang\) with a recursively enumerable axiomatization \(\mathrm{A}\) (after a conservative definitional extension by Theorem 2.20, if necessary):

  • if \(\mathcal{T}\) interprets induction-free Robinson arithmetic \(\mathsf{Q}\), then all computable relations are representable in \(\mathcal{T}\) and the Diagonal Lemma applies, whence \(\mathcal{T}\) is deductively incomplete (Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem);

  • if in addition the three Hilbert–Bernays–Löb derivability conditions for \(\mathrm{Prov}_{\mathrm{A}}\) are derivable in \(\mathcal{T}\) (for which interpretability of elementary arithmetic \(\mathsf{EA} = I\Delta_0 + \mathrm{exp}\), and a fortiori \(I\Sigma_1\), suffices), then the sentence \(\mathrm{Con}_{\mathrm{A}} \equiv \neg\mathrm{Prov}_{\mathrm{A}}(\ulcorner \bot \urcorner)\) (where \(\bot \equiv \neg(\theta_0 \to \theta_0)\) for some \(\theta_0 \in \Sent_\Lang\)), expressing the consistency of \(\mathcal{T}\), does not belong to \(\mathcal{T}\) (Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem).

The exact strength of the arithmetic and string systems sufficient for the special metalanguage of Part I of the PC paper itself is examined in the Conclusion.

3. Semantics and Models

3.1. Structures and Tarski Truth

In Section 3, the exposition passes completely to set-theoretic semantics: the metatheory freely uses sets, functions, and relations, and derivability \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\) from an arbitrary set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) is understood in the sense of § 2.4. Throughout the remainder, \(\Lang\) denotes a (finite or countable) signature.

Definition 3.1 (\(\Lang\)-structure and variable assignment). An \(\Lang\)-structure (or model of signature \(\Lang\)) is a tuple \(\Struct = \tuple{M, \{P^\Struct\}_{P\in\mathrm{Pred}_\Lang}, \{F^\Struct\}_{F\in\mathrm{Func}_\Lang}, \{C^\Struct\}_{C\in\mathrm{Const}_\Lang}}\), where:

  • \(M \neq \emptyset\) is a non-empty set called the domain (or universe) of \(\Struct\);

  • for each \(n\)-ary \(P \in \mathrm{Pred}_\Lang\), an \(n\)-ary relation \(P^\Struct \subseteq M^n\) is specified;

  • for each \(n\)-ary \(F \in \mathrm{Func}_\Lang\), an \(n\)-ary operation \(F^\Struct \colon M^n \to M\) is specified;

  • for each constant \(C \in \mathrm{Const}_\Lang\), a distinguished element \(C^\Struct \in M\) is specified.

A variable assignment in \(\Struct\) is an arbitrary map \(s \colon \FVar \to M\). For an assignment \(s\), a free variable \(a\), and an element \(m \in M\), \(s(a \mapsto m)\) denotes the assignment that agrees with \(s\) on all free variables except \(a\) and takes the value \(m\) at \(a\).

The value of a term \(T\) in \(\Struct\) under the assignment \(s\) (denoted \(T^\Struct[s] \in M\)) is defined by structural recursion: \[a^\Struct[s] = s(a), \qquad C^\Struct[s] = C^\Struct, \qquad F(T_1,\dots,T_n)^\Struct[s] = F^\Struct(T_1^\Struct[s], \dots, T_n^\Struct[s]).\]

Definition 3.2 (Truth of a formula in a structure). The relation of Tarski truth (or satisfaction) \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\) of a formula \(\varphi \in \Form\) in an \(\Lang\)-structure \(\Struct\) under a variable assignment \(s \colon \FVar \to M\) is defined by recursion on the number of connectives and quantifiers in \(\varphi\):

  • \(\Struct \models P(T_1,\dots,T_n)[s] \iff (T_1^\Struct[s], \dots, T_n^\Struct[s]) \in P^\Struct\);

  • \(\Struct \models (T = R)[s] \iff T^\Struct[s] = R^\Struct[s]\);

  • \(\Struct \models (\neg\varphi)[s] \iff \text{it is not the case that } \Struct \models \varphi[s]\);

  • \(\Struct \models (\varphi \land \psi)[s] \iff \Struct \models \varphi[s] \text{ and } \Struct \models \psi[s]\);

  • \(\Struct \models (\varphi \lor \psi)[s] \iff \Struct \models \varphi[s] \text{ or } \Struct \models \psi[s]\);

  • \(\Struct \models (\varphi \to \psi)[s] \iff \text{if } \Struct \models \varphi[s], \text{ then } \Struct \models \psi[s]\);

  • for quantified formulas \(\forall x\,\psi\) and \(\exists x\,\psi\), let \(b\) be the shortest (in number of symbols \(\pa\)) free variable not occurring in \(\psi\) (then \(\psi[b/x]\) is a formula of smaller complexity by Proposition 1.8 and Lemma 1.9): \[\begin{align*} \Struct \models (\forall x\,\psi)[s] &\iff \text{for every } m \in M,\ \Struct \models \psi[b/x][s(b \mapsto m)],\\ \Struct \models (\exists x\,\psi)[s] &\iff \text{there exists } m \in M \text{ such that } \Struct \models \psi[b/x][s(b \mapsto m)]. \end{align*}\]

A formula \(\varphi\) is true in the structure \(\Struct\) (written \(\Struct \models \varphi\)) if \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\) for every assignment \(s \colon \FVar \to M\); a formula is valid (written \(\models \varphi\)) if \(\Struct \models \varphi\) in every \(\Lang\)-structure \(\Struct\). For a set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) (or a finite list \(\Gamma\)), the notation \(\Struct \models \mathrm{A}[s]\) (respectively \(\Struct \models \Gamma[s]\)) means that \(\Struct \models \chi[s]\) for all \(\chi \in \mathrm{A}\) (respectively \(\chi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\)), and \(\Struct \models \mathrm{A}\) means that \(\Struct \models \chi\) for all \(\chi \in \mathrm{A}\); in this case \(\Struct\) is called a model of \(\mathrm{A}\) (in particular, a model of a theory \(\mathcal{T}\) when \(\mathrm{A} = \mathcal{T}\)). A formula \(\varphi\) is semantically entailed by \(\mathrm{A}\) (\(\mathrm{A} \models \varphi\)) if for every \(\Lang\)-structure \(\Struct\) and every assignment \(s \colon \FVar \to M\), \(\Struct \models \mathrm{A}[s]\) implies \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\).

Lemma 3.3 (Coincidence Lemma and Substitution Lemma). Let \(\Struct\) be an \(\Lang\)-structure and let \(s, s_1, s_2 \colon \FVar \to M\) be variable assignments.

  1. (a)

    (Coincidence Lemma.) If \(s_1(a) = s_2(a)\) for all free variables \(a\) occurring in \(T\), then \(T^\Struct[s_1] = T^\Struct[s_2]\). If \(s_1(a) = s_2(a)\) for all free variables \(a\) occurring in \(\varphi\), then \(\Struct \models \varphi[s_1] \iff \Struct \models \varphi[s_2]\). In particular, for a sentence \(\varphi \in \Sent\), truth \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\) does not depend on the assignment \(s\).

  2. (b)

    (Substitution Lemma.) For any terms \(T_0, T \in \Term\), formula \(\varphi \in \Form\), and free variable \(a\), one has \((T_0[T/a])^\Struct[s] = T_0^\Struct[s(a \mapsto T^\Struct[s])]\) and \[\Struct \models \varphi[T/a][s] \iff \Struct \models \varphi[s(a \mapsto T^\Struct[s])].\] In particular, for any quantified formula \(\forall x\,\psi\) (respectively \(\exists x\,\psi\)) and any free variable \(c\) not occurring in \(\psi\), truth \(\Struct \models (\forall x\,\psi)[s]\) is equivalent to \(\Struct \models \psi[c/x][s(c \mapsto m)]\) holding for all \(m \in M\) (respectively for some \(m \in M\)).

Proof.

(a) The first statement is immediate by structural induction on the term \(T\). The second is proved by induction on the number of connectives and quantifiers in \(\varphi\): the atomic case follows from the first statement, and propositional connectives preserve equivalence. For \(\varphi \equiv \mathsf{Q}x\,\psi\) and the shortest free variable \(b\) not occurring in \(\psi\), every free variable occurring in \(\psi[b/x]\) either equals \(b\) or occurs in \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\psi\); hence coincidence of \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) on the free variables occurring in \(\mathsf{Q}x\,\psi\) implies coincidence of \(s_1(b \mapsto m)\) and \(s_2(b \mapsto m)\) on the free variables occurring in \(\psi[b/x]\) for each \(m \in M\), and the induction hypothesis applies to \(\psi[b/x]\).

(b) The identity for terms \(T_0\) is proved by structural induction on \(T_0\). The equivalence for formulas is proved by induction on the number of connectives and quantifiers in \(\varphi\): the atomic case and Boolean connectives follow from the claim for terms and the induction hypothesis. Let \(\varphi \equiv \forall x\,\psi\). Observe first that for any free variable \(c\) not occurring in \(\psi\) and the shortest free variable \(b\) not occurring in \(\psi\), we have \(\psi[c/x] \equiv (\psi[b/x])[c/b]\); applying the induction hypothesis to the formula \(\psi[b/x]\) of smaller complexity yields \[\begin{align*} \Struct \models \psi[c/x][s(c \mapsto m)] &\iff \Struct \models \psi[b/x][(s(c \mapsto m))(b \mapsto m)] \\ &\iff \Struct \models \psi[b/x][s(b \mapsto m)] \end{align*}\] (the last equivalence follows from part (a), since when \(c \not\equiv b\) the variable \(c\) does not occur in \(\psi[b/x]\)). Thus the truth condition for \(\forall x\,\psi\) is independent of the choice of free variable \(c\) not occurring in \(\psi\).

Now choose a free variable \(c\) occurring in neither \(\psi\) nor \(T\) and distinct from \(a\). Then \(c\) does not occur in \(\psi[T/a]\), and word-for-word replacement gives \((\psi[T/a])[c/x] \equiv (\psi[c/x])[T/a]\). For any \(m \in M\), part (a) gives \(T^\Struct[s(c \mapsto m)] = T^\Struct[s]\) (as \(c\) does not occur in \(T\)), and since \(c \not\equiv a\), we have \((s(c \mapsto m))(a \mapsto T^\Struct[s]) = (s(a \mapsto T^\Struct[s]))(c \mapsto m)\). Applying the induction hypothesis to the formula \(\psi[c/x]\) of smaller complexity and the assignment \(s(c \mapsto m)\) for each \(m \in M\) yields the required equivalence: \[\Struct \models (\forall x\,\psi[T/a])[s] \iff \Struct \models (\forall x\,\psi)[s(a \mapsto T^\Struct[s])].\] The case \(\exists x\,\psi\) is analogous.∎

3.2. Soundness and Completeness

Two principal metatheoretic results link syntactic derivability \(\proves\) with semantic entailment \(\models\).

Proposition 3.4 (Soundness of FOL). Let \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) and \(\varphi \in \Form\). If \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\), then \(\mathrm{A} \models \varphi\).

Proof.

By definition of \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\), there exists a finite list \(\Gamma\) of formulas from \(\mathrm{A}\) such that \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\) in the sense of Definition 2.6. Fix an arbitrary \(\Lang\)-structure \(\Struct\) with domain \(M\). By induction on the derivation of \(\Gamma \proves \varphi\), we show that for every assignment \(s \colon \FVar \to M\) such that \(\Struct \models \Gamma[s]\), one has \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\).

  • Axiom basis (D1): propositional axioms are true under every assignment \(s\) by the definition of truth for \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to\) via the classical Boolean operations on \(\{0,1\}\). Equality axioms are true: reflexivity \(T = T\) is obvious, and for the congruence schemas \((T = R) \to (T_0[T/a] = T_0[R/a])\) and \((T = R) \to (\psi[T/a] \to \psi[R/a])\), the equality \(T^\Struct[s] = R^\Struct[s]\) entails \(s(a \mapsto T^\Struct[s]) = s(a \mapsto R^\Struct[s])\), whence Lemma 3.3 (b) yields \((T_0[T/a])^\Struct[s] = (T_0[R/a])^\Struct[s]\) and \(\Struct \models \psi[T/a][s] \iff \Struct \models \psi[R/a][s]\). For the quantifier axiom \(\forall x\,\psi[x/a] \to \psi[T/a]\) (where \(x\) does not occur in \(\psi\)): \(a\) does not occur in \(\psi[x/a]\) and \((\psi[x/a])[a/x] \equiv \psi\), so by Lemma 3.3 (b) the condition \(\Struct \models (\forall x\,\psi[x/a])[s]\) means \(\Struct \models \psi[s(a \mapsto m)]\) for all \(m \in M\), in particular for \(m = T^\Struct[s]\), which by the same lemma is equivalent to \(\Struct \models \psi[T/a][s]\). The axiom \(\psi[T/a] \to \exists x\,\psi[x/a]\) is verified dually.

  • Hypothesis basis (D2): if \(\varphi \trianglelefteq \Gamma\), then \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\) by the assumption \(\Struct \models \Gamma[s]\).

  • Modus Ponens (D3): from \(\Struct \models \chi[s]\) and \(\Struct \models (\chi \to \varphi)[s]\), Definition 3.2 immediately yields \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\).

  • Bernays' rules (D4): suppose \(\Gamma \proves \psi \to \chi\), \(a\) occurs in neither \(\Gamma\) nor \(\psi\), and \(x\) does not occur in \(\chi\). For an arbitrary \(m \in M\), the assignment \(s(a \mapsto m)\) agrees with \(s\) on all free variables occurring in \(\Gamma\) and in \(\psi\). By Lemma 3.3 (a), \(\Struct \models \Gamma[s(a \mapsto m)]\), whence by the induction hypothesis \(\Struct \models (\psi \to \chi)[s(a \mapsto m)]\). If \(\Struct \models \psi[s]\), then again by Lemma 3.3 (a) we have \(\Struct \models \psi[s(a \mapsto m)]\), and hence \(\Struct \models \chi[s(a \mapsto m)]\) for all \(m \in M\). Since \(a\) does not occur in \(\chi[x/a]\) and \((\chi[x/a])[a/x] \equiv \chi\), Lemma 3.3 (b) gives \(\Struct \models (\forall x\,\chi[x/a])[s]\). The case \(\exists x\,\psi[x/a] \to \chi\) is checked analogously.

Because for all \(\Struct\) and \(s\) the condition \(\Struct \models \mathrm{A}[s]\) implies \(\Struct \models \Gamma[s]\), it follows that \(\mathrm{A} \models \varphi\).∎

Theorem 3.5 (Gödel's Completeness Theorem). Let \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) and \(\varphi \in \Form\). If \(\mathrm{A} \models \varphi\), then \(\mathrm{A} \proves \varphi\).

Remark 3.6 (Relation to the detailed proof of completeness and main corollaries). A detailed proof of the Completeness Theorem (via Henkin's method) is presented in the companion note “The Henkin Construction”.

Combined with soundness (Proposition 3.4), the Completeness Theorem yields two fundamental corollaries about first-order models:

  1. (1)

    Compactness Theorem: a set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) has a model (i.e., \(\Struct \models \mathrm{A}[s]\) for some \(\Struct\) and \(s\)) if and only if every finite subset \(\mathrm{A}_0 \subseteq \mathrm{A}\) has a model. Indeed, choose an arbitrary formula \(\chi_0 \in \Form\) (e.g., \(a = a\) in FOL with equality or \(P(a,\dots,a)\) in FOL without equality) and set \(\bot \equiv \neg(\chi_0 \to \chi_0)\). If \(\mathrm{A}\) has no model, then \(\mathrm{A} \models \bot\), whence by Theorem 3.5 \(\mathrm{A} \proves \bot\), i.e., \(\Gamma \proves \bot\) for some finite list \(\Gamma\) of formulas from \(\mathrm{A}\); by Proposition 3.4, the finite set \(\mathrm{A}_0 \subseteq \mathrm{A}\) of formulas occurring in \(\Gamma\) satisfies \(\mathrm{A}_0 \models \bot\), and therefore \(\mathrm{A}_0\) has no model.

  2. (2)

    Downward Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem: if a set of formulas \(\mathrm{A} \subseteq \Form\) has a model, then it has an at most countable model (since the signature \(\Lang\), and hence the set of formulas \(\Form\), is at most countable, a model is constructed on equivalence classes of terms in the Henkin construction; for uncountable signatures, not treated in the present note, the upper bound on the cardinality of the model becomes \(|\Lang| + \aleph_0\)).

3.3. The Propositional Calculus as a Fragment of the Predicate Calculus

The propositional calculus (PC) admits two representations within first-order logic. In the first, the connectives of PC remain logical connectives, propositional variables become constants of the domain (elementary propositions), and the passage from the domain to truth values is effected by a single unary predicate; PC thus appears as a quantifier-free fragment of FOL. In the second, formulas of PC become terms, connectives become function symbols, and derivability and equivalence of formulas become relations among elements of the domain; this formalizes the algebraic semantics of PC (Part III of the PC paper).

Throughout this subsection, \(\vdash_{\textup{PC}}\) denotes derivability in PC (§ II.3 of the PC paper), and \(p_1, p_2, \dots\) denote pairwise distinct propositional variables (corresponding to the class \(\PVar\)). Because any finite list of PC formulas contains only finitely many variables, the signatures introduced below may be taken to be finite when dealing with concrete \(\Gamma\) and \(\mathcal{A}\).

Encapsulation: PC as quantifier-free FOL. Let the signature \(\Lang_0\) consist of an infinite family of constants \(C_1, C_2, \dots \in \mathrm{Const}_{\Lang_0}\), representing elementary propositions in the domain, and a single unary predicate symbol \(P \in \mathrm{Pred}_{\Lang_0}\) (\(\mathrm{Func}_{\Lang_0} = \emptyset\)), acting as a formal truth predicate (“the proposition is true”). To each formula \(\mathcal{A}\) of the language of PC is assigned a formula \(\mathcal{A}^*\) of the language of FOL in signature \(\Lang_0\) by replacing each variable \(p_i\) with the atomic formula \(P(C_i)\): \[p_i^* \equiv P(C_i), \qquad (\neg\mathcal{A})^* \equiv \neg\mathcal{A}^*, \qquad (\mathcal{A} \circ \mathcal{B})^* \equiv (\mathcal{A}^* \circ \mathcal{B}^*), \quad \circ \in \{\land, \lor, \to\}.\] By Definition 1.5, the formulas of the form \(\mathcal{A}^*\) are precisely the closed quantifier-free formulas of equality-free FOL in signature \(\Lang_0\), and the map \(\mathcal{A} \mapsto \mathcal{A}^*\) is bijective. For a list \(\Gamma = \mathcal{C}_1, \dots, \mathcal{C}_k\) in PC, one sets \(\Gamma^* = \mathcal{C}_1^*, \dots, \mathcal{C}_k^*\).

No individual variables occur in \(\mathcal{A}^*\), so the truth of \(\mathcal{A}^*\) in an \(\Lang_0\)-structure \(\Struct = \tuple{M, P^\Struct, \{C_i^\Struct\}_{i\ge 1}}\) does not depend on the assignment \(s\) (Lemma 3.3 (a)) and is determined solely by the conditions \(C_i^\Struct \in P^\Struct\) (Definition 3.1). In other words, an \(\Lang_0\)-structure \(\Struct\) induces a two-valued valuation \(\varepsilon_\Struct\) in the sense of the PC paper via \[\varepsilon_\Struct(p_i) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } C_i^\Struct \in P^\Struct,\\ 0, & \text{if } C_i^\Struct \notin P^\Struct, \end{cases}\] and every two-valued valuation \(\varepsilon\) arises in this way from the structure \(\Struct\) with domain \(M = \{0, 1\}\), predicate \(P^\Struct = \{1\}\), and constants \(C_i^\Struct = \varepsilon(p_i)\); moreover, structural induction on \(\mathcal{A}\) verifies \[\Struct \models \mathcal{A}^* \iff \varepsilon_\Struct(\mathcal{A}) = 1.\]

Proposition 3.7 (Encapsulation of PC in FOL). For any list \(\Gamma\) of PC formulas and any PC formula \(\mathcal{A}\), \[\Gamma \vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A} \iff \Gamma^* \proves \mathcal{A}^*,\] where the right-hand side denotes derivability in FOL of signature \(\Lang_0\) (with or without equality).

Proof.

Suppose \(\Gamma \vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A}\). Replacing each formula \(\mathcal{B}\) in a PC derivation by \(\mathcal{B}^*\) carries axioms of PC to axioms of group 1 of Definition 2.1, hypotheses from \(\Gamma\) to hypotheses from \(\Gamma^*\), and applications of Modus Ponens to applications of rule D3; this yields a derivation \(\Gamma^* \proves \mathcal{A}^*\).

Conversely, suppose \(\Gamma^* \proves \mathcal{A}^*\). By Proposition 3.4, \(\Gamma^* \models \mathcal{A}^*\). Let \(\varepsilon\) be a two-valued valuation such that \(\varepsilon(\mathcal{C}) = 1\) for all \(\mathcal{C} \trianglelefteq \Gamma\), and let \(\Struct\) be the \(\Lang_0\)-structure with \(M = \{0, 1\}\), \(P^\Struct = \{1\}\), and \(C_i^\Struct = \varepsilon(p_i)\). Then \(\Struct \models \Gamma^*\), whence \(\Struct \models \mathcal{A}^*\), i.e., \(\varepsilon(\mathcal{A}) = 1\). Therefore \(\Gamma \models_{\mathbb{B}} \mathcal{A}\), and by Post's theorem (§ III.4 of the PC paper), \(\Gamma \vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A}\).∎

Thus PC coincides with the fragment of closed quantifier-free formulas of equality-free FOL in signature \(\Lang_0\), and derivability in FOL on this fragment is conservative: a derivation of \(\mathcal{A}^*\) in FOL making arbitrary use of quantifiers and equality proves nothing beyond what is derivable in PC. On the other hand, adding quantifiers in signature \(\Lang_0\) even without equality produces statements about the domain such as \(\exists x\,P(x)\) or \(\forall x\,P(x)\) that do not reduce to PC formulas, while in FOL with equality statements about the cardinality of the domain and distinctness of elementary propositions also appear, such as \(\exists x\,\exists y\,\neg(x = y)\) or \(\neg(C_1 = C_2)\).

Embedding into the domain: the theory of Boolean algebras. Let the signature \(\Lang_{\mathsf{BA}}\) consist of the function symbols \({\sim}\) (arity \(1\)), \(\sqcap\), \(\sqcup\), \(\Rightarrow\) (arity \(2\)) and the constants \(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\); it contains no non-logical predicate symbols (\(\mathrm{Pred}_{\Lang_{\mathsf{BA}}} = \emptyset\)), and the sole relation of the language is logical equality \(=\). The operation symbols are distinct from the connectives \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to\), because function symbols of a signature cannot coincide with logical symbols of the alphabet (Definition 1.3). Infix metalanguage notation \(T \sqcap R\), \(T \sqcup R\), \(T \Rightarrow R\), \({\sim}T\) is used for terms, and \(T \leqslant R\) abbreviates the atomic formula \((T \sqcap R) = T\). The order could also be introduced as a binary predicate symbol of the signature with the axiom \(a \leqslant b \leftrightarrow (a \sqcap b) = a\); the resulting theory differs only in notation.

Let \(\mathsf{BA}\) denote the theory of Boolean algebras: the finite list of equalities of signature \(\Lang_{\mathsf{BA}}\) expressing the laws of a distributive lattice with least element \(\mathbf{0}\), greatest element \(\mathbf{1}\), and complement \({\sim}\), together with the equality \((a \Rightarrow b) = ({\sim}a \sqcup b)\). The equality axioms are not included in this list: they are logical (group 3 of Definition 2.1). The models of \(\mathsf{BA}\) are precisely Boolean algebras in the sense of § III.3 of the PC paper (including the one-element algebra).

To each variable \(p_i\) is assigned the free variable \(a_i\), and to each formula \(\mathcal{A}\) of PC is assigned a term \(T_{\mathcal{A}}\) of signature \(\Lang_{\mathsf{BA}}\): \[\begin{gather*} T_{p_i} \equiv a_i, \qquad T_{\neg\mathcal{A}} \equiv {\sim}T_{\mathcal{A}}, \\ T_{\mathcal{A}\land\mathcal{B}} \equiv T_{\mathcal{A}} \sqcap T_{\mathcal{B}}, \qquad T_{\mathcal{A}\lor\mathcal{B}} \equiv T_{\mathcal{A}} \sqcup T_{\mathcal{B}}, \qquad T_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}} \equiv T_{\mathcal{A}} \Rightarrow T_{\mathcal{B}}. \end{gather*}\] If \(\mathfrak{B}\) is a Boolean algebra viewed as an \(\Lang_{\mathsf{BA}}\)-structure, then an assignment \(s \colon \FVar \to \mathfrak{B}\) of free FOL variables determines a valuation \(\varepsilon_s(p_i) = s(a_i)\) of PC variables taking values in \(\mathfrak{B}\); every PC valuation arises in this way, and structural induction on \(\mathcal{A}\) verifies \[T_{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathfrak{B}}[s] = \varepsilon_s(\mathcal{A}).\] Under this representation, PC formulas become elements of the domain, and assertions about them become atomic equality formulas.

Proposition 3.8 (Algebraic representation of PC). For any list \(\Gamma = \mathcal{C}_1, \dots, \mathcal{C}_k\) of PC formulas and any PC formula \(\mathcal{A}\), \[\Gamma \vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A} \iff \mathsf{BA} \proves (T_{\mathcal{C}_1} \sqcap \dots \sqcap T_{\mathcal{C}_k}) \leqslant T_{\mathcal{A}},\] and for empty \(\Gamma\): \(\vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A} \iff \mathsf{BA} \proves T_{\mathcal{A}} = \mathbf{1}\). In particular, \(\vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A} \leftrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) if and only if \(\mathsf{BA} \proves T_{\mathcal{A}} = T_{\mathcal{B}}\).

Proof.

By the Deduction Theorem (§ II.3 of the PC paper), \(\Gamma \vdash_{\textup{PC}} \mathcal{A}\) is equivalent to \(\vdash_{\textup{PC}} (\mathcal{C}_1 \land \dots \land \mathcal{C}_k) \to \mathcal{A}\), and by the completeness theorem with respect to the class of Boolean algebras (§ III.4 of the PC paper), this is equivalent to \(\varepsilon(\mathcal{C}_1) \land \dots \land \varepsilon(\mathcal{C}_k) \to \varepsilon(\mathcal{A}) = 1\) for every Boolean algebra and every valuation \(\varepsilon\) in it. By the lemma on implication in a Boolean algebra (§ III.3 of the PC paper) and the identity \(T_{\mathcal{B}}^{\mathfrak{B}}[s] = \varepsilon_s(\mathcal{B})\), this means that \((T_{\mathcal{C}_1} \sqcap \dots \sqcap T_{\mathcal{C}_k}) \leqslant T_{\mathcal{A}}\) is true in every model of \(\mathsf{BA}\) under every assignment, i.e., \(\mathsf{BA} \models (T_{\mathcal{C}_1} \sqcap \dots \sqcap T_{\mathcal{C}_k}) \leqslant T_{\mathcal{A}}\). By Theorem 3.5 and Proposition 3.4, the latter is equivalent to derivability of this formula from \(\mathsf{BA}\). The case of empty \(\Gamma\) and the equivalence claim follow in the same way.∎

The theory \(\mathsf{BA}\) formulates within FOL what in Part III of the PC paper was formulated in the set-theoretic metatheory: equivalence of formulas is expressed by equality, derivability by order, and the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra \(\mathsf{LT}\) is the free model of \(\mathsf{BA}\) on the countable generating set \([p_1], [p_2], \dots\). Adjoining quantifiers and FOL connectives over equalities allows properties of individual models to be expressed that cannot be expressed by PC formulas: the axiom \(\neg(\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{1})\) excludes the one-element algebra, and the axioms \(\neg(\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{1})\) and \(\forall x\,(x = \mathbf{0} \lor x = \mathbf{1})\) together characterize the two-valued model \(\mathbb{B}\) up to isomorphism.

Correspondence dictionary. The table below compares the notions of PC and their images under the two representations. The middle column differs from the first only in casting elementary propositions as atoms \(P(C_i)\), as expressed by Proposition 3.7; the right column is the encoding of the algebraic semantics of PC in the language of FOL.

Conclusion. The Postulate of Binarity and the Spiral of Metatheories

In Part I of the PC paper, a special metalanguage of finite words was carved out of natural language, encompassing operations on words (§ I.1), generation of classes of words (§ I.2), and general statements and induction on the construction (§ I.3). For a substantive study of any formal calculus—proving unique readability, closure under substitution, the Deduction Theorem, and finitary consistency—the induction principle remains indispensable. The analysis below does not abandon induction as a working metatheory, but uncovers the internal stratification of Part I of the PC paper itself: within it emerge successively an operational core of generation and verification of concrete strings (§§ I.1–I.2, stage 0), general statements without induction (the beginning of § I.3, stage 1), and the full finitary metalanguage with structural induction (§§ I.1–I.3 in full, stage 2), followed by set-theoretic semantics (Part III of the PC paper and Section 3 of the present paper, stage 3).

The postulate of binarity. The pre-formal foundation of the special metalanguage of Part I of the PC paper is the postulate of binarity in two inseparable manifestations:

  1. (1)

    Symbolic binarity: the capacity to distinguish at least two non-coinciding symbols (\(\partial \not\equiv \varrho\), \(\mathtt{0} \not\equiv \mathtt{1}\)). Over a one-letter alphabet \(\{|\}\), concatenation is commutative (\(|^m |^n \equiv |^n |^m\)) and reduces to addition of lengths, yielding decidable Presburger arithmetic. Introducing a second distinguishable sign qualitatively transforms the structure: non-commutativity of adjoining (\(\partial\varrho \not\equiv \varrho\partial\)) and positional coding appear, whereas further expanding a finite alphabet from \(2\) to the \(16\) symbols of \(\Alf\) reduces to block coding by four-bit nibbles (\(16 = 2^4\)) and adds no new expressive power.

  2. (2)

    Logical binarity: bivalence of the outcome of elementary word comparison (“identical / distinct” in § I.1, “true / false” in § I.3 of the PC paper) and the rigidly fixed sense of the metalanguage connectives (“not”, “and”, “or”, “if …, then”).

Evolution of recursive rules and closure conditions. Recursive definitions of word classes of the form “basis—rules—closure” (§ I.2 of the PC paper) do not presuppose a strong metatheory precisely because the final clause “no other words belong to the class” changes its logical status as the metatheory ascends:

  • at the pre-formal stage 0 (§§ I.1–I.2 of the PC paper), the rules serve solely as templates for step-by-step verification of a finite sequence of exhibited words, and closure acts as a restrictive norm of admission (a word is admitted to the class only upon exhibiting its finite construction); as noted already in § I.2 of the PC paper, such verification relies only on inspecting words as in § I.1 and invokes neither the logic of general statements nor induction from § I.3;

  • upon adding quantifiers at stage 1 (the beginning of § I.3 of the PC paper), closure turns into an explicit \(\Sigma_1\)-definition of membership via existence of a construction code: \(\xi \in K \iff \exists d\,\mathrm{Build}_K(d, \xi)\);

  • upon adding induction on the construction at stage 2 (§§ I.1–I.3 of the PC paper in full), closure unfolds as a schema of structural (or level) induction, allowing one to prove general statements \(\forall \xi \in K\,S(\xi)\);

  • upon adding the axiom of infinity at stage 3, closure takes the classical set-theoretic form of the least fixed point \(K = \bigcap \{X \mid \mathrm{Base} \subseteq X \land \mathrm{Step}(X) \subseteq X\}\).

The spiral of metatheories and retrospective verification. The axiomatization of a stronger theory can already be written down as a finite text at stage 0, without yet possessing its deductive power. A qualitative increment occurs at the next step, when the constructed system is adopted as the new active metatheory and turned downward to verify and prove the consistency of the preceding stage:

  1. Stage 0.

    Generation (quantifier-free operational core, §§ I.1–I.2 of the PC paper). By means of concatenation, word-for-word replacement, and verification of exhibited strings, the syntax and inference rules of PC and FOL (terms, formulas, axioms, derivations) are specified and the axioms of formal theories (\(\mathsf{TC}\), \(\mathsf{PA}\), \(\mathsf{HF}\), \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)) are written down, still without appealing to general statements or induction from § I.3 and without proving general metatheorems.

  2. Stage 1.

    Quantification without induction (\(\mathsf{TC} \equiv \mathsf{Q}\)). Adjoining to the operations of § I.1 the universal and existential statements from the first half of § I.3 of the PC paper (“for all words”, “there exists a word”) prior to introducing the induction principle—formally, adopting FOL quantifiers over the axioms of concatenation (associativity, the editor property \(\xi\eta \equiv \zeta\theta \implies \xi \equiv \zeta \lor \exists\omega\,(\xi\omega \equiv \zeta \lor \zeta\omega \equiv \xi)\), and indivisibility of symbols of a finite alphabet)—yields A. Grzegorczyk's theory of concatenation \(\mathsf{TC}\) (Grzegorczyk, 2005), mutually interpretable (via sequence coding following W. Quine, 1946, or the hexadecimal codes of Remark 2.22) with induction-free Robinson arithmetic \(\mathsf{Q}\). Turning back to stage 0, the level \(\mathsf{TC}/\mathsf{Q}\) provides \(\Sigma_1\)-representability of the classes \(\Term\), \(\Form\), \(\Ax\), \(\Thm\), the Diagonal Lemma, undecidability of FOL, and Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem. In the absence of induction, however, neither totality and uniqueness of word-for-word replacement \(\xi[\zeta/\eta]\), nor unique readability (Proposition 1.8), nor the Deduction Theorem, nor finitary consistency of \([\emptyset]_\Lang\) is provable here.

  3. Stage 2.

    Induction over the finite (\(\mathsf{TC} + \mathrm{Ind} \equiv \mathsf{PA} \equiv \mathsf{HF}\); finitary minimum \(I\Sigma_1 \equiv_{\Pi_2} \mathsf{PRA}\) and \(\mathsf{EA}\)). Including induction on the construction (§ I.3) closes the full special metalanguage of Part I of the PC paper (§§ I.1–I.3), and extending the induction schema to all first-order formulas yields the full theory of finite objects in three pairwise bi-interpretable forms (Ackermann, 1937; Grzegorczyk, 2005): the theory of concatenation with the induction schema \(\mathsf{TC} + \mathrm{Ind}\), Peano arithmetic \(\mathsf{PA}\), and the theory of hereditarily finite sets \(\mathsf{HF}\) (\(\mathsf{ZF}\) with the negation of the axiom of infinity and \(\in\)-induction).

    The proofs of Sections 1–2 use the lower, finitary fragment of this stage, marked by three exact features: (a) because of rules F4 and D4, induction goes beyond proper subwords to a numerical measure—quantifier-connective depth of formulas (\(\psi[c/b]\) in Lemma 1.9, \(\chi[b/x]\) in the valuation \(v\) of § 2.4 and in the translation \((\mathsf{Q}x\,\psi)^*\) of Theorem 2.20) and derivation length (in Proposition 2.12 (a) after Lemma 2.7); (b) inductive hypotheses carry free parameters (\(T, a, \Delta, \chi\)) with parameter swapping and shifting inside the inductive step (in Lemma 1.7 (b) and under the double substitution \([c/b]\), \([T/a]\) in Lemma 1.9); (c) when classes are literally specified by an unbounded \(\Sigma_1\) existential quantifier over constructions, this basis coincides with the arithmetic \(I\Sigma_1\), which by the Parsons–Mints–Takeuti theorem (Hájek, Pudlák, 1993) is \(\Pi_2\)-conservative over primitive recursive arithmetic \(\mathsf{PRA}\) (the boundary of Hilbert's finitism according to Tait, 1981), and upon writing explicit exponential code bounds narrows to elementary arithmetic \(\mathsf{EA} = I\Delta_0 + \mathrm{exp}\) (pure \(I\Delta_0\) without \(\mathrm{exp}\) is insufficient because of \(2^n\) truth tables in PC and iterated substitutions).

    Turning downward, stage 2 completely verifies the syntax of stage 0 (parsing, substitution, deduction, eliminability of definitional extensions, finitary consistency of \([\emptyset]_\Lang\)) and proves the consistency of the induction-free theories of stage 1 (\(\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{TC})\), \(\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{Q})\) are already derivable in \(\mathsf{PRA}/I\Sigma_1\)), yet by Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem it cannot prove its own consistency \(\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{PA})\).

  4. Stage 3.

    Actual infinity (\(\mathsf{ZFC}\); thresholds of countable semantics \(\mathsf{WKL}_0\) and \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\)). Since the theory of finite sets \(\mathsf{HF}\) is already built at stage 2, passing to the set-theoretic metatheory \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) reduces to adopting the axiom of infinity \(\mathrm{Inf}\) (together with the power set and choice axioms over infinite sets). In terms of reverse mathematics (Simpson, 2009), two thresholds of second-order arithmetic appear within Section 3: constructing a Henkin model and the Completeness and Compactness Theorems for countable signatures are equivalent over \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\) to the subsystem \(\mathsf{WKL}_0\) (Weak Kőnig's Lemma over \(\Sigma_1\)-induction, which is \(\Pi^0_2\)-conservative over \(\mathsf{PRA}\) by H. Friedman's theorem), whereas defining the full Tarski truth predicate \(\Struct \models \varphi[s]\) over an arbitrary infinite structure and carrying out the general soundness induction correspond to the system \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\) (whose first-order part coincides with \(\mathsf{PA}\)).

    At the level of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), the totality of finite objects of stage 2 is gathered into a single actually infinite set (\(V_\omega \models \mathsf{HF}\), \(\omega \models \mathsf{PA}\)), yielding proofs of \(\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{PA})/\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{HF})\), general first-order model theory, and comparison of arbitrary theories, whereas the question of \(\mathrm{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) passes to the next turn of the spiral (to large cardinal axioms or the hierarchy of Type universes of the Lean kernel from § 1.3). Meanwhile, \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) itself is written as a recursive axiom schema in the \(16\)-symbol syntax of stage 0, closing the loop of the spiral (Fig. 6).

Thus the postulate of binarity serves not as a single axiom from which all of mathematics is deductively derivable—Gödel's theorems rule out the existence of such a closed basis, and each transition to the next stage of the spiral (quantification over a potentially unbounded domain of words, closing finite iteration into an induction principle, reifying an infinite process into an actually infinite set) is an independent act of idealization logically underivable from the preceding one—but rather as the minimal a priori threshold of discursive thought. Precisely herein lies the exact separation between the two levels of the basis: the postulate of binarity together with the operational core of §§ I.1–I.2 of the PC paper provides the minimal symbolic support sufficient to write down and execute formal rules, whereas the full special metalanguage of §§ I.1–I.3 with structural induction forms the minimal deductive metatheory required to prove the soundness of those rules. Even when constructing many-valued, intuitionistic, or modal calculi, the metalanguage of their syntax and rule verification remains strictly two-valued. Below the threshold of distinction in sign and in judgment, neither formal language, nor proof, nor counting is possible; above it—already without expanding the original two-bit vocabulary—unfolds the entire inexhaustible spiral of mathematical theories and metatheories.
